On June 8 she will put to sea from Halifax on the first of two local cruises lasting until

Inquiries of the Ministry
June 24. These will concentrate on the training of reserve personnel. An annual leave period for the first watch will follow.
On August 2 Warrior will sail for the United Kingdom to ferry personnel of No. 803 and 825 squadrons. These are the men who will man the new Sea Fury and Firefly IV aircraft of H.M.C.S. Magnificent when she is commissioned. A number of R.C.N. (reserve) men, doing annual training, will also be carried.

This group will probably consist of one complete scout troop numbering about 35. Accommodation could not be arranged for these groups on passenger vessels, and as the Warrior was making the trip anyway their passage could be undertaken without additional expense.
Warrior will return to Halifax, at the end of August, when the annual leave period for the second watch will begin. Between October 1 and October 21 she will be at sea for deck landing training. This will be carried out by No. 883 and 826 squadrons, manning her Seafires and Firefly I's. speechtext:
Perhaps I might give some information which was promised at an earlier sitting in reference to tin. With the concurrence of my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), under whose jurisdiction the non-ferrous metals administration of the wartime prices and trade board comes, I wish to make a statement to the house on tin supplies. Hon. members will recall that last week I made a brief reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Stephenson) on the subject and promised to add to it later.
The current shortage of tin in Canada arises out of sharply reduced output from the Malayan field which is the principal world source of the metal. When Japan controlled this area during the war a great deal of damage was done to tin mining facilities and it is expected that not until well into 1949 will production in Malaya be up to standards prevailing before the Japanese occupation.
Allocation of available world tin supplies is determined by the combined tin committee, an international body which sits periodically in Washington. Canada became a member of the committee in the session of March of this year. At that session the Canadian delegate was Mr. Clark Wilson, then deputy administrator of non-ferrous metals, a capable and dependable officer with many pre-war years of experience in the metals industry.
At the March meeting of the tin committee,, because of the gloomy outlook for supplies,, the committee was able to allocate to Canadar for the first half of this year, a bare 55 per cent of our minimum estimated requirements. This quantity, to correct my statement last Tuesday, represented only about 40 per cent of our allocation for the corresponding period of 1946. when world stocks were heavily drawn upon.
In the face of this situation it has been necessary to maintain a careful supervision over releases and uses of tin. Hon. members will realize that our food pack and dairy industries are heavily dependent on supplies of this metal. It is absolutely indispensable in modern industry. As may be imagined, the authorities concerned have been hard put to it to look after essential consumers as well as to keep the less essential manufacturers supplied at least on a minimum operating basis. Nevertheless, for the first four months of this
Inquiries oj the Ministry

year, Canadian industry received more tin than in the same period last year. This was accomplished, of course, by drawing upon stocks. To date, so far as we know, nobody has had to shut down.
Our purchases in past weeks have been rather more encouraging and we have reason to hope that the position will gradually improve. The next meeting of the combined tin committee is the middle of this month and our delegate is being instructed to press strongly for a greatly increased quota.

speechtext:
Right. lion. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution :
That it is expedient to present a bill to amend The Prairie Farm Assistance Act, 1939, to provide that the two schedules of payment now provided under the emergency year section and the crop failure section be merged and become payable in a ly year without specific authority from the governor in council and without requiring that a minimum number of townships be eligible before the crop failure schedule of award is payable; that the restriction in respect to the payment of awards to farmers with a certain min;-mum production of wheat may be removed; and that certain provisions be clarified in order to facilitate administration.
He said:	The resolution on the order
paper is one providing for the introduction

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
of a bill to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. 1 believe there will be general agreement in the house with regard to the amendments proposed.
Sections 3 and 4 in the present act provide for payments of certain amounts on an acreage basis, in a year when the government declares it an emergency year, under section 3, and when it is declared to be a crop failure year, under section 4. The proposed amendments do away with the necessity for the government's declaring any year an emergency year. They also do away with the necessity for there being any number of townships over and above one in order to have it declared a crop failure year.
The provision for two different ranges of payments is entirely done away with, and the measure will operate automatically. If there is one township or more in which there is a yield of eight bushels or less, payment will be made on the basis provided in the amended act. The only difference in the basis of the provision is that section 3 did provide for payment in the lower category, or from four bushels down, while section 4 provided for payment from five bushels down. Payment as it was made for five bushels down, in the act as it was, will now be made from four bushels down and will go into effect automatically in every township in which there are four bushels or less. That is the principal change made by the amending bill. The provision now in the act whereby any farmer in a township where payment was made, who had over three thousand bushels of wheat, was denied payment, is taken out, so that no matter what bushelage he has, he is entitled to payment.
Some other amendments are designed to clarify the meaning of the act and to bring into effect the provisions of which I have spoken. These, however, are the two main amendments.
It is my intention that as soon as the bill is printed and prepared for second reading it will be referred to the committee on agriculture. Any questions which hon. members desire to ask or any proposals they wish to make with respect to the measure may be discussed fully in committee and of course can be discussed on second reading of the bill if the house so desires. However, the suggestion that the bill go to a committee would perhaps provide a reason why the principal discussion, for the time being, might take place there. I would suggest that the resolution go now to the committee of the whole.

subtopic: CROP FAILURE PAYMENTS-AWARDS TO FARMERS WITH MINIMUM PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the statement by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) this afternoon, and I believe we in this group can approve the changes he has intimated are likely to take place in the act. I had a resolution placed on the order paper this year asking that the provision of the act be extended. I believe when we are considering prairie farm assistance we should consider making it applicable to other parts of Canada-for instance to the fruit growers in the Niagara peninsula of Ontario, the fruit growers of British Columbia, the tobacco growers of Ontario, and the fruit growers of the maritime provinces. All these would receive a good deal of benefit if the act were extended, and if benefits were paid on account of crop failures to all farmers in Canada suffering such failures.
This year, on account of the lateness of the season, many counties in Ontario and Quebec are likely to experience widespread crop failures, perhaps the worst in the history of the area. I should hope that consideration might be given to the extension of the act so that farmers throughout the country may have adequate protection from crop failures.
I am interested in this legislation, too, because I represent a constituency in the Palliser triangle, the area in which this act has been of greatest benefit to the farmers.
Prairie Farm Assistance Act

It has been stated in the house on various occasions that the settlement of that area was a mistake. Let me say that large production of grain and dairy and meat products has come from that area, so that the whole of the Palliser triangle forms an important part of the agricultural producing area in Canada and contributes heavily in agricultural products for the nations of the world.
There are many faults in the present act and certainly the changes that have been suggested will be welcomed. We hope that more changes will be made when the bill is presented to the house.
This act now provides some measure of security to the farmers. The government stated many times at the dominion-provincial conference that it would do everything possible to provide the people of this country with security. For instance, one of the statements in the government proposals was this:
In familiar terms, our objectives are high and suitable employment and income and a greater sense of public responsibility for individual economic security and welfare.
And again:
The dominion government feels it has a responsibility to assist the industry (meaning agriculture) in making the necessary readjustments to peace time circumstances and to work in cooperation with the provincial governments to provide for a greater degree of stability in farm income and a greater measure of security than has prevailed in the past.
The bringing of this legislation before the house at this session will give the government a chance to show the people whether or not they are really going to give the farmers security. The present provision for a possible payment of $2.50 per acre on half the cultivated acreage, or a maximum payment of $500, is not giving our farmers security. We in this group recommend that the benefits be increased to at least $6 per acre, that they be paid on an individual basis and that if necessary the deductions be increased so that more money may be paid into the fund for extending these benefits.

subtopic: CROP FAILURE PAYMENTS-AWARDS TO FARMERS WITH MINIMUM PRODUCTION
speechtext:
There may be a lot of "car-rieds", but I do not care where they come from. This is an important resolution and I intend to speak on it.
I have made a calculation of what I consider to be the minimum cost of carrying out farming operations on an average farm in southwestern Saskatchewan. The cost of farming is cheaper per acre in this part of the province than in any other part, but the cultivated acreage is larger, so I have no doubt the total cost per farm will compare reason-
[Mr. Argue.J
ably well. The average size of farm is 325 acres. Under the act a farmer can receive $2.50 per acre on half of his cultivated acreage, which would make his payment approximately $400. It will take at least 200 bushels of wheat to seed 162 acres at a cost of $240. It will cost not less than 75 cents per acre, or $121.50, to seed those 162 acres. Summerfallowing operations will cost 75 cents per acre and for two operations $243. The total seeding and summer-fallowing costs are more than 1600. On the basis of the payments received under the P.FA.A. on a crop of less than four bushels per acre this average farmer will be $200 in the red on his seeding and summer-fallowing operations. He would not have one dollar from the fund to provide for the payment of taxes and interest on his debt, to say nothing of providing for the cost of his own living and the maintenance of his family.
To increase the payments to $6 per acre would provide a maximum payment of $1,200. or a payment to the average farmer of approximately $1,000. If that increased payment was provided for in the act it would be little enough in view of the great increases which have taken place in farm costs. These increases have taken place because the government saw fit to remove the price ceilings. The increased farm costs are directly a result of the action of the government. Therefore I contend it is the responsibility of the government to see that the farmers are protected in time of crop failure.
There is another reason why the payments should be increased. I refer to the decision of the supreme court outlawing the Saskatchewan farm security act. The Department of Justice of this government took that act to the supreme court where it was declared to be ultra vires. That act meant a lot to the farmers of Saskatchewan in time of crop failure. If a man had a $5,000 mortgage and his interest rate was six per cent, the farm security act would have saved him $300. Many farmers are going to have increased expenses in years of crop failure because that act has been disallowed. If this government believes in giving the farmers security then it must give some additional compensation. It took that act to the supreme court and by doing so was instrumental in having it disallowed.
I contend that the payments under this act should be made on an individual basis, because making the payments on a township basis is not fair. I have had dozens and dozens of cases brought to my attention in which farmers have had complete crop, failures and perhaps lived just across the road from

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
a township in which payments were made, but they did not receive payment because there were not enough other farmers in the immediate vicinity who were also in the unfortunate position of having crop failures.
The present act provides that payments will be made in an area of one-quarter of a township provided that it is a rectangle and provided that one side lies along a township receiving the bonus. I had a case brought to my attention this year in which there were nine sections or one-quarter of a township with less than eight bushels per acre. Eight of those sections formed a rectangle but the ninth, which was necessary to bring them under the act, made it impossible to form a rectangle and therefore the farmers were not eligible for payments. Because of that regulation those farmers who justly deserved payments were discriminated against. The only way that situation can be overcome is to provide for payments on an individual basis.

Mr. Speaker, as the bill to be based on this resolution is to be sent to a committee, I shall be brief. This group is glad that the government has seen fit to bring in the resolution at this time. We were very much disappointed last year when owing to pressure of business the government decided not to bring it in then.
Seventy-five per cent of my constituency might be classified as a semi-permanent drought area. Therefore the people in that district are dependent upon the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and I think will continue to be dependent upon it until such time as the government sees fit to construct the irrigation projects which have been promised for a number of years but which the government seems reluctant to begin. Irrigation has been
Prairie Farm Assistance Act

constantly in the minds of those people since the early settlement days, and year after year the government has promised that these irrigation projects will be constructed, but so far the people have looked in vain for their commencement.
In spite of all the criticism that has been made of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and its administration, I believe it has served the people well. To many farmers it has made all the difference between being able to carry on and having to give up. Most of the criticism I have heard has been of a constructive nature and directed chiefly against the method of determining whether or not certain land is eligible for payment of the bonus. That is the main criticism in the area I come from. The minister will agree that the method is far from satisfactory. When the act was first introduced the minister suggested that after a while it might be possible to determine eligibility on the basis of the type of soil a farmer owned, but so far that method has not been introduced, and I can see that it would not be an easy way of determining eligibility for the bonus.
The two points the farmers criticize are these. In a township that is not eligible it is possible to take out a minimum of nine sections of land, provided they are contiguous to a township that is eligible, and provided further that the sections are in a rectangular block. There may be sections right alongside the block with yields of less than four bushels to the acre, yet because they are not within the rectangular block they are not eligible for the bonus. This year I ran into a peculiar case-it may not happen very often-which showed how unsatisfactory this method of determining eligibility of the land is. I had a township referred to me that was declared eligible. Then the inspector found within the township six sections which had a high yield. The act does not provide for taking six sections out of a township. It provides for taking out only nine. So they included three sections which had had a total crop failure along with the six, and then took those nine out. Naturally the farmers on the three sections which had suffered a crop failure within a township that had been declared eligible felt bitter when denied the bonus by reason of being included in a block of nine sections, only six of which had a high yield. That may not happen very often, but it should not be necessary for the inspector to include three sections which had a total crop failure along with six others which had a good crop.
We in this group welcome the changes proposed by the minister, and I hope that 
when the bill is before the committee he will allow a full discussion of other points which we think should be dealt with.

The house resumed from Monday, June 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ilsley for the second reading of Bill No. 177 to amend the Penitentiary Act, 1939.

Approximately eight years have elapsed since the former minister of justice told the house of the deplorable conditions associated with penitentiary administration. How much has been done since the house, at his request, passed a bill for the appointment of three commissioners, I do not know; apparently very little. We have been told that the reason for that is that there is a certain amount of dual responsibility as between the provinces and the federal government in the matter of prison care and reform, and all matters pertaining to criminology. But I cannot see why the federal government itself, in the interim of the past eight years, could not have set apart one of its own penal institutions for the adoption of what the minister of that day strongly recommended, namely, the Borstal system of reform. The Borstal system, of course, is nothing more or less than the reclamation of prisoners, and that is an important feature.
I have made an exhaustive study into the operation of the Borstal system, but I am not going to talk about that today; I have done so before. I have visited in the, old country many prisons in which this system is in operation.
I spent eight or ten hours in one of the Borstal institutions, thoroughly surveying everything pertaining to their programme. While there I made it my business to inquire from the various prisoners, with the permission of the guards who were taking me around, why it was they were there. Many of them were fine looking, and it was amazing to me to see such well set-up young men incarcerated in a penal institution. On my return home I made a survey following up

Penitentiary Act
what I had learned from the few prisoners with whom I discussed the matter. Anyone representing in a large city a riding such as mine, containing approximately 60,000 to 70,000 people, has had the experience which has been mine, over the past eighteen years, of being interviewed by fathers and mothers, husbands and wives, sisters and brothers in reference to their dear ones who had in some way fallen afoul of the law and been sent to prison. After I came home from my last investigations into the Borstal operations in the old country I started to make inquiries of everyone who called to see me about getting this one or that one released or the term of imprisonment shortened. In many cases I went to the prison itself where the person the people had called to see me about was incarcerated, and I asked him-they were mostly males; in fact I do not remember having talked to any females-how he had fallen from grace, and I began writing down the reasons which were given. One of the main causes was that the prisoners came from homes which were broken up, for one of the many reasons why such things happen, and therefore they did not have a proper home training. I pursued that study, because I felt that while the Borstal system is essentially a reclamation system, it would be much better if we could get behind that and get back to the time before the young man was sent to prison and required reclamation through the Borstal system.
An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.

Having in mind a programme of prevention, I studied each individual case with which I came in contact; and it was not an easy matter. It took a long time to do it, but I have been at this a long time, Your Honour. Prison reform and reclamation of prisoners have been studies of mine for many years. I have always been interested in the solving of human troubles.
As I said a moment ago, the broken home was number one reason given for young men being sent to prison. Therefore whatever programme the new commissioner puts into operation, as a beginning I hope he will study the question of how to get back beyond the reclamation period to the school days.
This brings me to my second thought. In addition to the lack of a desirable home environment in which a boy or a girl would receive the good advice and instruction of happy and contented parents, I found that there was lack of education. I was amazed to find that so many of our young offenders have so little education. I took that matter up with 83166-2381
one of the Ontario reformatory boards, and was astonished at the account they gave of the lack of education and mental deficiency. Speaking of mental deficiency, which goes along with lack of education, I had a conversation with the head of the mental hygiene council, as I believe it is called, to which this house every year-and rightly so in my judgment-votes a matter of $10,000. The head of that council is Doctor Hincks. who is perhaps one of the best versed men in America in mental hygiene. I learned from him that in his judgment from thirty to forty per cent of the young folks going to school today are to a certain extent mentally deficient. That condition can be cured or arrested if the proper facilities are provided. The deficiency in mentality of youth, which results in their being sent to prison, is a problem which should be studied by the new commissioner. How it is to be overcome I do not know. We might spend ten or perhaps twenty million dollars in building new penal institutions for reform, but if it is not too late we might do better to spend $20,000,000 in looking after our youth before it became necessary to be concerned about their reclamation. One way of doing that would be to assist such institutions as the mental hygiene board and that celebrated authority on mental hygiene, Doctor Hincks. In this way we might do something to lessen crime on the part of our youth.
In the Ontario reform reports I find the statement made that 10-03 per cent of those incarcerated in penal institutions are mentally deficient. That is a tremendous toll. Not only are they unable to return any benefit to their country, being mentally deficient ; they are a cost to the country when it becomes necessary to send them to a reform institution, following the commission of some crime. That is another side of the prevention programme. It was stated also that 14-9 per cent were right on the border. I have observed that myself in my own humble investigations. I have often said to myself. "Well, it is a wonder this one did not commit murder or some grievous crime," instead of some misdemeanour that was not so serious. That makes a total percentage of 24-12 either mentally deficient or right on the border. There is something wrong with our institutions if these figures are correct, as I have no doubt they are. It would seem that we are far behind the programme of the Borstal reclamation system. Further it is stated that 32-79 per cent were dull, and we have all seen that. I have made it my business to speak to many young men in prison, in the common gaols and from there right up to the penitentiaries. I have visited their homes and talked to theii
Penitentiary Act

parents, who in too many cases also are dull. Of course often a dull child comes from dull parents, though that is not always the case since many of the very finest parents have dull children. But if they are dull they should have some chance to attain efficiency and understanding, so they will not commit crimes. That makes a total of those dull, on the border and below the border of 56-91 per cent. That is simply incredible, and I can only say that a proper system of training probably would save many of them from going to gaol. I believe that if mental hygiene were properly carried out and extended, many of the youth of the land could be kept from committing crimes.
I find further that of the people who are normal, 62-8 per cent did not receive any further education than the sixth grade. I found that too in the prisons in England, in talking to the young men there. Their education was woefully deficient. That is a pretty serious situation. How it is going to be overcome I do not know, but as the former minister said, it is a staggering problem and costs the country a staggering sum. But the cost is far greater when such people make no return. If they can be saved before they commit a crime that will send them to gaol, whatever the cost to the country it will be money well spent.
Then take a look at our book stands, and see the literature for sale there. Much of what you see is very light literature; but in addition to what is on the book stands there are many other places where youth can get literature that is not fit for anyone to read. If this is not a federal matter I wonder if the provinces should not take note of the fact that much of the literature offered for sale today certainly is not fit for our youth to read. When we were young we had many excellent books to read. Those books are still available today, and if their cost could be reduced by printing thousands of them so that every youth in the land could read them, it might have a very wholesome effect. I do not think an}- child could read the like of "David Copperfield" or "Barnaby Rudge" or "Edwin Drood", or other works of Dickens and other equally well known authors, without a beneficial effect. Many of these books, however, are rather high priced, so our young people buy a cheaper book or a magazine which adds nothing at all to their intelligence. I feel that we may be derelict in our duty to this country in not seeing to it that our young people have proper literature to read, for I

believe this would reduce the number who later might be sent to our gaols and penitentiaries.
There is another example connected with my own youth about which I was not going to say anything, but I have decided to mention it after all. That is the lack of family worship, which is nothing short of monstrous. In my home the bible was read every morning; one or other of my parents would lead in prayer, and naturally this had a wholesome effect on each member of the family. We respected them the more because of their desire to see that we walked the right way of life. Today, however, that is lacking to an extent that is nothing short of shocking. What can we expect but an increase in crime when too many of the youth of today have little direction along the right, path?
Then where can our children play today? Where are the playgrounds in our cities? If a child of my neighbourhood wants to play in a park he has to go at least half a mile; and that is in the city of Toronto. It is all right if the children live next door to the park or in the next street but in my neighbourhood it is a long way to a park. Yet children must play. If they play in the streets they hear many things they should not hear. Of course many of them go to the supervised school playgrounds, but the children do not like to play on gravel or on hard cement, so those playgrounds are not very popular and the children play anywhere they can. In England, even though their population is very much congested and they have not anything like the land we have here, on a holiday you will find all the roads leading from London and the other cities filled with people either in motor cars or on bicycles going to what they call the commons. There are commons everywhere; that is one thing I like very much about the old country, and those commons are full of people. I suppose the name "commons" has come down through the centuries, but these open spaces are full of people enjoying themselves.
I often say to myself:	If the fathers and
mothers of Toronto want to go out on a Saturday or a Sunday afternoon, where can they go? If they come to a shady little spot with a creek running through, and some sand, they find a fence arount it with a sign, "Trespassers prohibited." I would like to see throughout Ontario and in all the other provinces for that matter, hundreds of the areas like the "commons" they have in England. They would call them commons; here they might be called something different, but the purpose and use would be just the same.

Penitentiary Act
They would be recreation areas to which fathers and mothers could drive on a Saturday or a Sunday. They could enjoy being out in the fresh air with the children. There is nothing like God's great outdoors to make people think rightly.
I have travelled far and wide in remote areas. I have gone over mountains and rivers. I love to travel there because I see God and His handiwork everywhere. And so would the children see it, too. But they have to get out of the cities to see it.
In a constituency the size of mine there are many boys and girls who get into trouble. Many parents, sisters and brothers come to see me about those who have gone astray. I always try to find out the reason for their having made these mistakes.
I hope the new commissioner and those associated with him will take these things into account. At the moment their job may be one of reformation. But can we not start earlier than that, and set up a system of prevention? There are ways of preventing crime. Better to spend $10 million on prevention, on places for children to play, on parks; better to spend $10 million on slum clearance, where people are living under such congested conditions that their children have no place to play. Far better to spend those millions of dollars for prevention than to have to spend an equal amount-as we will have to do-on the building of prisons, to put boys and girls where they cannot do any good for their country or for themselves.
I often wonder what would happen in this country if it were not for that mere handful of men and women, that small number of devoted men and women throughout the country, some of whom are to be found waiting at the prison gates for the prisoners as they come out. And when I say this I think of the Salvation Army and those associated with other religious organizations who assist those who are being turned out of the prisons. I often wonder what this country would be like if that handful of men and women did not give some attention to those who leave our prisons.
I had a case brought to my attention recently which caused me considerable concern. It was in connection with a fine man with a wife and family. He had been a bookkeeper, and for some reason-the reason is neither here nor there-he took some of his employer's money. He had been in that man's employ for twenty-one years, and that was his first lapse. It should not have occurred, of course; but some impelling motive forced him to take that money, with the result that
he was sent to the reformatory at Guelph for some length of time. Had he been sent to the penitentiary it would have been even worse.
I have often thought we should have some fund or some system through which those who have been guilty of some misdemeanour, probably committed out of desperation, could be helped instead of being sent to some institution. I am not in favour of criminals being at large, of course; and I believe in the principle that corrective punishment should be meted out where it is due. But I have in mind some method of prevention whereby, so that instead of a man being sent to a place where he can do nothing to help his wife and children he would be prevented from getting into trouble in the first instance. Perhaps that aspect of the matter has not been studied to any great extent by crime preven-tionists, but it is worthy of diligent study, and something might come of it.
I know of a fine young man who did something foolish. Certainly he should not have done it; he should have stood his ground rather than run away. Upon being captured, as he rightfully was, he was sent to prison. After serving eighteen months he was released. This young man had not committed what could be classified as a crime; he was not that type of man. Upon his release from prison, with the knowledge that up and down the years I had obtained jobs for many young men in like circumstances, he came to see me. On many occasions young men who have come from prison have asked for my assistance, and ' I have always been delighted to try to get them jobs. I would stake my own reputation on their behalf, and if necessary I would give a guarantee that I would be responsible for their good conduct. I spoke about this young man to some people I knew well, referring to the time he had served in prison. I have forgotten how long it was-perhaps twelve or eighteen months-but I could not get him a job. Finally I went to a manager and told him it was just as much his responsibility as mine to give this boy a chance to start life again. If I could not have got him a job soon after his release from prison, what could he be expected to do? He had not committed any great crime in the first instance, but there was no telling what he might do if evervone turned him down.
There is another point to which the Minister of Justice might give some thought, and which would give help to those coming out of prisons. It has been shown in England that from 60 to 70 per cent of first offenders who obtain positions upon their release from prison, and
Penitentiary Act

who thus have some money coming in to take care of their personal necessities, do not engage in crime again. It must be understood however that first of all they must get a job. 1 know many men and women in Toronto who are engaged in trying to secure jobs for those who come out of the prisons. I have done a considerable amount of that work myself.
I always tell young men who are released from prison not to pass by a policeman as if he were going to give chase or make an arrest. I urge them to stop and talk to the police, and to tell them their problems. The police in Toronto are anxious to prevent crime, and I have no doubt that the same would apply to other cities. Our former chief of police in Toronto, Chief Draper, spent years doing that kind of work, and he did a fine job in assisting those who were released from prison. Surely this would be another means of prevention of crime.
I hope that whoever is in charge of the programme of reclamation will give some thought to suggestions of this kind. The only reclamation system in operation today is the Borstal system. It is doing a mighty fine job, but it does not apply to hardened criminals. First offenders should not be put in with hardened criminals. The penitentiaries branch might well set apart one of the penitentiaries where first offenders serving sentences up to five years, we will say, could be incarcerated, so that they w'ould not come in contact with the hardened criminals who cannot be reformed.
I do not know' what should be done for these later. Perhaps I am too soft-hearted to wish severe punishment to be inflicted upon anyone. An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of [DOT]cure. I am firmly convinced that the Borstal system can do a big job in reformation of prisoners, but I want to get behind the necessity for reclamation. I want to get to the youth of this country. I do not know how it is going to be done, but I certainly would like to participate in it myself.
The Ontario government is doing a good job at the present, time. The provincial secretary, under whose jurisdiction these matters come, was sent to England. As far as I could see from the press reports he pretty well followed the trip I made. He visited Leeds prison, the prison at Glasgow, the original florstal prison and different prisons in the 'London area. I felt complimented when I saw -that. I do not say that he followed my itinerary, but it looked like it. He came back convinced that as far as first offenders go the Borstal system can do a grand work. I know it can. because I have seen it in operation.
JMr. MacNlcol.]
I notice the Ontario government has purchased 600 acres in the vicinity of Ottawa which I presume will be used as a boys' farm, a first offenders' farm or something like what they have outside of Glasgow. It should do a good work. The Ontario government have schools at Galt and Bowmanville and other places to which first offenders are sent. I say again that the federal government cannot enter any field in which the province now is but can make their own application of the Borstal system to first offenders sentenced to two years imprisonment and over. I was glad to read a few days ago that 'the Quebec government is also starting to promote reclamation, perhaps along the same lines as they are doing in Ontario, with schools and farms. I wish them every success, as I wish Ontario every success.
I am sincere in what I have said, and I am intensely earnest in the belief that there should be some means of prevention to reduce the number of those who are sent to prison. If that does not prevent crime, there should be some such system as the Borstal system which has proven so satisfactory and which has been adopted almost universally throughout the world for the reclamation of first offenders.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Before the hon. member sits down I should like to correct him. He has made the statement two or three times that the Borstal system applies to first offenders. It does not. On page 201 of the report it is stated:
It should be emphasized that no first offenders are as a rule sent to Borstal institutions. They are not for novices in crime but for those young offenders who have failed to respond to other courses of treatment.
How old is that report?

I think you will find they have advanced since then because I was informed by the officials in charge of the prison at Glasgow that many of those there were first offenders. I am only taking the information given to me by those associated with the reclamation work. I do not see why it should not apply to first offenders sentenced to two years and over, as well as to first offenders sentenced to eighteen months.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Just to get this right, I quote again from the report:
Youths between 16 and 23 years of age, when brought before the court, are divided roughly into three classes:	those who are not bad
enough for Borstal, i.e., who can be dealt with by probation or other non-institutional treatment, those who are too bad for Borstal, and the balance, mostly proved recidivist offenders, who are selected for Borstal treatment. It

Penitentiary Act
should be emphasized that no first offenders are as a rule sent to Borstal institutions. They are not for novices in crime but for those young offenders who have failed to respond to other courses of treatment.

When I visited the Borstal institution in England they gave me pamphlets dealing with the reclamation of those who were brought to their prisons. In those pamphlets it was pointed out very clearly that this one or that one was a first or a second offender. They stated that the number of third offenders had been reduced. In any event, those who are sentenced to the penitentiary for two. three or more years might be reclaimed if kept apart from hardened criminals and given the benefits of the Borstal system. What is there about the Borstal system that they should not have? There is nothing that I know of. I watched it at work in the various prisons; I discussed the matter with their teachers, and I cannot see anything but benefit that would derive from the application of this system. Most persons who commit a crime are reformable, leaving out of consideration the hardened criminal, through the application of the Borstal system.

Mr. Speaker, the bill at present under study deals only with the change in the set-up of the penitentiary commission as provided in the Penitentiary Act, 1939. It is intended to change the number of commissioners from three to one and to provide for the appointment of two deputy commissioners. The sections of the 1939 act concerning the appointment of assistant commissioners are not changed, as well as other sections of the act, A single authority of one commissioner is to replace that of a board of three commissioners, but two deputies are to act directly under him. That appears simple enough and it might call only for an expression of opinion as to the merits of a one-man show or a three-man board. The debate which has followed the introduction of this legislation has covered the whole question of penitentiary administration and penal reform. I think that is most commendable because, with the introduction of the present bill, is brought forward again the whole problem of our penal system in Canada. I do not think too much can be said about the urgency of bringing it in line with improvements in penology throughout the world. Hon. members who have spoken from all sides of the house have shown a public spirit and a keen sense of appreciation of the gravity and urgency of the situation.
It may be distasteful to hear anyone speak of his previous experiences and make personal
references during the course of the debate, but I find myself in the awkward predicament of having to do this in order to justify myself and to substantiate certain opinions which I may express. During the last six years I have received numerous letters from people who have devoted much of their lives to this question. They have expressed their disappointment at my silence over the years. I must confess that there are letters which I have not dared to answer because I would have had to admit the opportunism which had prompted me to stay silent.
The people who wrote to me, and others, knew of my long association with the Department of Justice and my great interest in such questions as the handling of prisoners, the reform of criminals and the general administration of our penitentiaries as well as the necessity of reorganizing our whole penal system. Many of these people were in contact with me at the time when my efforts were directed toward the entire remodeling of our penal set-up. Therefore I feel it my duty to acquaint the house with some aspects of the problem as I know and understand them.
I do not want to pose as an expert in such matters but, as the solution of this problem should be the concern of all of us, I think we must all contribute within our limitations our share to its solution. The present bill providing for a reorganization of the administrative set-up of Canadian penitentiaries is intimately connected with the vast problem of how can we best organize and administer our penal system; how can we best deal with those who have violated our criminal laws; how can we act to curb recidivism and orientate our penal system so as to reform criminal offenders and liberate the country from the burden of mounting costs of handling those whose first incarceration has failed to reform them, if it has not launched them in a career of crime?
As I proceed with my remarks I trust the minister will be able to dissociate himself from a common ministerial habit of considering as personal criticism any remarks made about a branch of his department or about the civil servants or officials who are responsible therefor. During my long association with ministerial activities and observing the house under other governments, I have found that this is an attitude which is unfortunately too often taken by some members of cabinets. It is an attitude that is not conducive to good government, which demands free and open discussion of any and *11 angles of the administration's policy, not only from the opposition parties, not. only from different
Penitentiary Act

groups who try to find something wrong with the government, but from government supporters. Yet the latter, faced with such an attitude, are often prone to hesitate to utter remarks which, while critical, would be in the interests of better administration. It is a well known fact to most of us that many departmental officials rely on the popularity and respect enjoyed by their minister to save them from any severe scrutiny of their acts. That does not apply particularly to one department but to most of them. The speed with which a minister's estimates or bill is passed is considered a great feat by his officials and as more or less of a criterion of the popularity of the minister. But I am convinced that the Minister of Justice has not that unhealthy attitude and that it will never be a part of his mentality.
Before I go on with my remarks, I should like to congratulate the minister upon, having at last brought this measure before us, which means the reorganization of the penitentiaries branch. This is only a first step and it took a long time to come, but at last we are getting moving and, I think, in the right direction.
If I may be permitted I should like to read from a lecture which I myself gave some time ago. If I did not explain that I might be reproached for reading my speech.
In 1910 Mr. Churchill, who was then Home Secretary in Great Britain, laid down the proposition, which received the approval of all those qualified to speak on the question, that the degree of civilization to which a nation had attained could be measured by the way in which it treated its lawbreakers. By that test Canada does not stand as high as it should. For a full understanding of Canada's situation respecting prison administration I might be permitted to review a few historical facts.
Shortly after the Act of Union in 1842, a prison board was created to inspect and administer all gaols, prisons, and hospitals in the united provinces, including the penitentiary at Kingston. This board found an almost unbelievable situation, even for that day and age. I am making that, reference to 1842 and afterwards shall compare conditions then with conditions in 1947. Even if I might be thought to be going too far back in history, it is relevant to the problem, because some of the problems brought before that prison board have not yet been solved after 105 years, and are still receiving our attention. As I said, this board found an almost unbelievable situation, even for that day and age, to exist in the local gaols an<^ prisons of the provinces, and a great unwillingness on the part of local authorities to invest any money in improving [Mr. Picard. 1
conditions. After a bitter struggle and the exercise of considerable patience, however, the board finally achieved its purpose. It then turned to the improvement of the penitentiary at Kingston. In the performance of these two tasks, it became obvious that the great, problem was the reclamation of young offenders, for whom no fitting quarters were then available. The board turned, therefore, to the establishment of reformatories, which in those days were places devoted to reformation and not, as now, merely places of incarceration.
I say that, because some of our institutions have been called reformatories when to all intents and purposes they were just still gaols or penitentiaries as all the others were.
In Lower Canada, a reformatory was established at lie aux Noix, which was later moved to St. Vincent de Paul. In Upper Canada, a reformatory was established at Penetan-guishene. A hospital for mental cases was also constructed at Kingston, Rockwood hospital, which is still in existence. The period wTas one of awakening social consciousness in all countries and by 1867 the board had made the Canadian penal system one of the best in the world, at least as compared with Great Britain and the United States.
The British North America Act brought an end to many of the hopes of the penologists of that time. The architects of that act were engaged in the attempted solution of much greater problems and. in seeking this solution, lost sight of the effect on penal administration of the division of powers made between the federal government and the provinces. Jurisdiction over gaols, reformatories, and hospitals was given to the provinces, while the federal government was given jurisdiction over the penitentiaries only. An arbitrary distinction came to divide these institutions. Any sentence under two years involved imprisonment in a provincial or local institution, and any sentence of two years or over involved imprisonment in a penitentiary. This arbitrary division of jurisdiction destroyed the uniformity of treatment applied to lawbreakers.
The royal commission which reported in 1938 realized the fatal defects of the division of jurisdiction brought about by the British North America Act and recommended that all penal institutions be replaced under one authority, the new penitentiary commission. This is, of course, a matter for constitutional amendment based on agreement between the provincial and federal governments. Whether or not it can be realized remains to be seen. Reading the report of the new commissioner, General Gibson, one realizes that his conversations have not been such as to give him

Penitentiary Act
much hope that most of the provinces will agree, except perhaps the maritime provinces. Yet this is something we should be working upon to try to attain and it may be attained in the years to come, even if it is not of immediate concern to us in the matter of the reorganization provided for in the bill.
Sir John Thompson was Minister of Justice from September, 1885, to December, 1894. Almost alone among ministers of justice until the advent of the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, he was interested in penal reform. I am making this reference to a man whom I have served and with whom I have been in the Department of Justice. Prior to Mr. Lapointe, Sir John Thompson was the Minister of Justice who gave the most personal interest to this question. Sir John Thompson was aware that Canadian penitentiaries were not properly equipped to deal with the reformation of young offenders and he conceived the establishment of a reformatory institution for this purpose. To this end he purchased a site near Cornwall, Ontario, had blueprints drawn and approved, and arranged for the purchase and manufacture of building supplies and equipment. Before the completion of the project, another minister of justice supplanted him, through what historical fact I do not know. The new minister referred the matter to the deputy minister of justice of that day and asked for a report on the inception and progress of the new institution. It has been my experience that reports of commissions are prone to die or lie a long time on the desk of a deputy minister or some other official. That is what happened in this case. I think the deputy minister reported to the new minister that this was a whim of his predecessor, and the whole project was scrapped. This was the last attempt to have special reformatories under the federal government up until the time when the Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe in 1926 announced his intention of doing something. He said in the House of Commons on May 31, 1926:
There is another thing which is not made the subject of the resolution, but to which I am giving a good deal of thought, and that is the possibility of segregating the young convicts who are sentenced for the first time. If wre could find a way to build a special institution, or even two institutions for the purpose of receiving and keeping these young men rather than put then with hardened criminals, I think that would be a good reform to undertake.
Three years later funds had been granted by parliament for the construction of two institutions, one of which was Collins Bay and the other Laval building near Montreal. I might say that work started to. proceed on both these
institutions, but after the short Liberal eclipse of 1930 to 1935 when the late minister, Mr. Lapointe, came back to the house, little had been done. Twenty years after the project was started, Laval is not completed. Collins Bay was completed but has served not directly for the purpose it was intended. I will discuss later, on an item in this year's report of the superintendent, the claim that Collins Bay has been made a reformatory or that it has reclaimed people or made it so .that they would not be sentenced again; in fact that they will be reformed better than under the Borstal institution. We shall have these figures in a short while. Today, 105 years after the first penitentiary board reported on the unsatisfactory conditions of penitentaries for the treatment of young criminals we are exactly or, let us say, 99-9 per cent where we were 105 years ago. We are still discussing the opportunity of segregating reformable persons. We are told that we shall have real reformatories. That is why I am so glad to see that this measure is brought before the house now. I repeat, this is the first good move made in a long while.
If anyone thinks, after a survey or a close study of our penal institution systems, that they have been operated according to the discoveries of experienced penologists throughout the world and in comparison with those of the United States and especially Britain, I cannot see how he can arrive at this conclusion. The two major trends concerning the administration of penitentiaries are based on different theories of penology. The first that prevailed up to the last part of the nineteenth century was purely the punitive aspect of incarceration. The second that has gained more supporters throughout the world since 1875, and especially since the beginning of the century is that the punitive is only one aspect, but the reformative is the essential one if one wants to avoid the curse of recidivism. As the Archambault report states at page 9:
Entirely apart from humanitarian ground*, and. from a purely economic point of view, and for the eventual benefit of society, the task of the prison should be, not merely the temporary protection of society through the incarceration of captured offenders, but the transformation of reformable criminals into law-abiding citizens, and the prevention of those who are accidental or occasional criminals from becoming habitual offenders.
Although in Great Britain, as well as in certain parts of the United States, much has been done toward the efficient reformation of the inmates, it is sadly to be admitted that to many of those who have visited and inspected the Canadian penal system, in Canada little has been done in that regard. That
Penitentiary Act

is said, despite the statement which 1 mentioned a moment ago, and which I shall look into, about the claims that Collins Bay has reformed the people who were sent there.
In last year's report of the superintendent, figures are given which were ably analysed by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), which still stand, and are ample evidence that we have not yet advanced far in the right direction. I shall avoid going into any details of the royal commission's report, but I commend the reading of it to all those interested in the problem. After reading it, few I am sure would not come to the conclusion that it is a splendid piece of work.
In my opinion there are three main sources of inefficiency in our penal administration. The first is the wrong or the punitive attitude of the penitentiary officials and of the departmental authorities, up to a very recent time which could, be counted in months; second, the incompetence and lack of vision of most of the men connected with the administration; and, third, the wrong attitude of all authorities as well as of succeeding governments throughout the years for the building programmes of the penal institutions, and also toward the implementing of recommendations which have been made by different commissions from time to lime. This may appear to be simplifying the problem too much; but I think all that goes wrong in the system can be traced back to one of these three causes. Had we the proper reformative attitude, coupled with the necessary punitive methods, many of the wrongs outlined in the report would soon be corrected, provided that the second cause was also corrected and that the incompetent officials were removed or that some of the departmental attorneys assigned to penitentiary matters were removed or reassigned to other duties. There would remain then the necessity for the government to understand that to erect a building by convict labour on antiquated plans cannot be coupled with an efficient tackling of the penal problem, and I shall deal with this in the final recommendations I shall make at the end of my remarks.
For a number of years prior to 1932 tne penitentiaries were administered by General Hughes. I was in the department while he was there, and I think I can say that I seldom agreed with the recommendations he made, many of which I did not find in the proper and right reformative spirit. Nevertheless I would pay this compliment to him. He was the only one who had a system and a method and operated it. He was succeeded afterwards by General Ormond, a most prom-

ising, hard working and sincere man, but not cut out for this type of work. Despite his effort, during his administration the mistakes of the past brought about serious conditions of unrest, and we know all the sad happenings, the riots, fires and so on. We owe, in fact, a great deal to a former member, Miss MacPhail, who, assisted by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) who spoke today, the former Minister of Justice, Mr. Lapointe, and a few others, aroused public opinion to such a point between 1930 and 1935 that there came about a general feeling that an investigation of our penal system was necessary.
I well remember in 1935 the late Norman Rogers, who was then a Liberal candidate in Kingston, telephoning me in Quebec to meet him in Kingston to discuss certain aspects of the problem. The moment he arrived there he had been faced with the question as a large number of his constituents in Kingston were interested directly in the penitentiary because they were employed there, or indirectly because some of them had relatives working there.
I had been in the department from 1925 to 1930, but at the time I was out of the service. Mr. Rogers subsequently pledged himself to look carefully into the problem and seek information from people who had been connected with the service. A few days after our meeting Mr. Rogers pledged himself to insist on a full investigation. It was the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) who, in 1935, promised the people of Canada that if his party wTere elected a free and impartial investigation of our penal system would follow.
The history of the penitentiary system of Canada has been one of recurring cycles. Neglect is followed by disturbances. Disturbances give rise to investigations, which are made and reported. The public believes, quite naturally, but erroneously, that once the causative evils are exposed they will be rectified. The officials of the Department of Justice, however, take it merely that they have weathered another storm and continue in the same old way until another cycle is started. We had investigations in 1876, 1913, 1920. 1937 and 1938. It is now time to stop going around in these vicious circles, and this can be done if the present commission or the present new set-up understands the situation fully and sets to work immediately in the right direction. There is no reason why the penal system of Canada should not be the best in the world. We have the example, which has been given to us by the British, of a system

which has been called a character reformer, and we have the example of what has been done in the United States. We could couple both with a better understanding of our problem and by drawing from the experience of these people, we could have one of the most efficient services in the world.
To revert to the history of our system, within six months after the present government came back to power in 1935 a commission of three men was appointed, consisting of Judge Arehambault, who had been a criminal lawyer in Montreal, a crown attorney for a number of years, a prominent jurist and a judge of great experience; Hon. Mr. Craig, a former attorney general of Manitoba and a man thoroughly acquainted with all such questions; and the present Chief Justice McRuer, who was then one of the most prominent attorneys in Toronto. These people made a report which, as J said a moment ago, everybody should read. This report is one of the milestones in the progress of penal reform. When the report was tabled, the minister asked to have changes made in the act. They were accepted here but refused in the senate. In the next year. 1939, he came back again. Unfortunately, the royal commission's report was more or less tabled and made inoperative, I would sajr, because of the strong influence of the departmental officials of the time, who did not believe in it. Some of them had been reproached by the report for their way of running the affairs of the penitentiaries. None were accused of ill faith, dishonesty or anything of that kind, but the report concluded that the attitude of these men was not a proper one to be held by those who were to run the penitentiary system. Yet these men were there, and they stayed there and prevented the report from being implemented. It may be said that the recommendations were not carried out on account of the war, and there is some ground for that. I would not want to go on and give the details about the prospective appointment of a commission in the first days of 1940, an attempt which failed because the one selected to be chairman finally changed his mind, and the one selected to be vice-chairman decided to run for parliament. Then at the end of 1940 another commission was under consideration. Again the prospective chairman, at the last moment, said his doctor advised against his acceptance of the appointment; since then he died. In 1941, the then Minister of Finance, who is the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) was rightly pressing the department to curtail expenses that were not of the utmost importance. That gave sufficient ground to
the departmental officials who were for the status quo to keep matters in abeyance and prevent anything from being done.
Last year, fortunately, an aroused interest in the country with regard to this question brought the matter to the attention of the then minister of justice, who decided to appoint a commissioner to look into the report of another commission. We now have that report before us. Between the bringing in of the report in 1938 and the present time, eight or nine years have elapsed. A great deal could have been done in that time. During that time we were most fortunate, in a certain way-although I suppose it cannot be said to be fortunate to have a war, but my remarks apply to the penitentiaries-in that people found employment, a large number of men went into the armed forces, and the penitentiary population was small, as was the case in most other wars.
Immediately at the end of the war or toward the end of it, a new crime wave started; our penitentiaries started to fill up again, and we were faced with the same situation as obtained before the war. But in that time, shall we say-and the commissioner himself mentions it in his report, but, of course, in diplomatic language-the former superintendent who had been blamed by the commission, was withdrawn from the service by the then minister of justice, Mr. Lapointe, in 1938. The commission was not yet appointed. One of the inspectors, Mr. Sauvant, acted as superintendent, and he was one about whom the commission had said they could not say much, that he had had no chance to prove what he could do, but on the other hand had not shown any special ability. One of the other inspectors, who had also been blamed by the report, was withdrawn. The third one had only accountancy experience and was more or less going around looking after the accounts; he was also supervising to a certain extent, without being experienced in that field, the industrial end of the penitentiary system. Soon after the war started, Mr. Sauvant, the inspector who was acting as superintendent, asked leave of absence to join the Free French forces. The remaining official, the accountant, asked leave to join the royal air force, and the third commissioner, Doctor George Shortt, who had been appointed on a temporary basis by Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe also left the branch. He had served as assistant secretary to the Arehambault commission, and was brought into the picture to help start a reorganization of the system. He was brought in because of his long and intimate connection with the Arehambault commission and his experience with social problems and investigations. He had been with the

combines investigation board and others of the kind. This gentleman also was seconded, some time afterwards, to the wartime prices and trade board; so at one time during the war, instead of a commission approved by parliament, instead of a superintendent and two inspectors, we had only a chief engineer running the whole show.
Today at last, after nine years, the minister brings in a resolution providing that we shall finally have a commission. It will be a one-man instead of a three-man commission. Our first reaction might be to see what General Gibson has done up to now. I must say that it seems to me he has made a thorough survey of the problem and has carefully read the files of the department and many of the memoranda prepared. In the interim, after the royal commission report was brought in, when I left the department, and When Doctor Shortt, who had been charged by Mr. Lapointe to deal especially with that problem, was left in the background, the old crowd gained influence anew and prevented any reform from being brought forward. General Gibson seems to have made a thorough survey of these reports and the suggestions made by Doctor Shortt and by the commission, and I think 'his report has much to commend it. Last, year many people smiled when the then minister of justice recommended that a commissioner be appointed to look into the report of a commission that reported on conditions in penitentiaries. But this year, after seeing General Gibson's report, I do not think it will be necessary to appoint a new commissioner to look into the report of the commissioner who looked into the report of the royal commission. So finally we have something on which we can work.
I do not think I have time enough to analyse the whole of General Gibson's report, but there are a few things which might be pointed out. The commissioner states at page 5 that the establishment of separate reformatory institutions for young offenders can be done only with the consent of the provinces.
I think this is just partly true, because there is nothing to prevent the penitentiary commission, if they wanted to put into effect one of the most important clauses of the Archambault report, from establishing a Borstal type of institution for young offenders. If such institutions were set up, well staffed, were as well organized as possible and were superior to provincial institutions, there is nothing to prevent judges from sentencing young offenders to these institutions in which they would be reformed, instead of sentencing them to two years, less one day, which means a sentence

to a local or provincial gaol, while a two years' sentence would send them to these new federal institutions. Then the parole board could take charge, if we got one that would also be revamped, as has been suggested bj the Archambault commission, or even if it remains as it is, because I believe it is much better than the penitentiary administration and is working very well under the present system, though not with the proper facilities for following up these people after they are released from gaol. However I believe this part of the department works well even under the present system, and this would permit these young offenders to be released when their reformation had reached the proper point, which would be at about the same time as they would be released from the gaol, and we would have in the country a sort of Borstal institution that would be worth while.

Does the hon.
member not think it would be advisable that every possible means of reforming these offenders should be attempted, while they are still young?

Of course, and I do not see that what the hon. member says conflicts in any way with what I am saying. I am advocating an institution for young offenders, a reformatory, instead of sending them to gaols. I want to give them a better chance to reform, and not continue as criminals.
The report itself states quite frankly that the reorganization has not been undertaken. Up to the present the yearly reports of the superintendent would lead us to believe that something had been done. They always included such words as ''when possible", "if possible", "to the extent possible", and so on; but I think the present commissioner is frank when he says it has not been undertaken. He gives a list of about twenty improvements having to do with the treatment of convicts which have been introduced as a result of the report of the royal commission, but I believe all these improvements were brought about within eighteen months after the report was presented and mainly through the efforts of Doctor Shortt and myself. These changes have not been made since 1939 or 1940; they were made in 1938 and 1939. Paragraph (f) states that convicts are now provided with lighters at public expense, and I understand that this was an improvement brought about by the acting superintendent, while all the others were the result of the study made by the temporary inspector, Doctor Shortt, who had knowledge of the work of the commission and was eminently qualified to do these things in the right way.

The report goes on. to deal quite frankly with conditions in the penitentiaries; but many of the improvements indicated, while they make a good showing, deal with such matters as new pigsties or new barns at this or that penitentiary, and have little bearing on the question of the reformation of criminals and the reorganization of the whole penitentiary set-up. They do nothing to decrease the incidence of crime or to help in the reformation of criminals, which my hon. friend mentioned a moment ago. These improvements have bettered the farm production and others have contributed, to relieve the harshness of the regime, but they are not improvements that will affect conditions in the penitentiaries for the betterment or reformation of individuals. In my opinion the present report is a great improvement over what we have seen in the past, and I have great confidence that General Gibson will get things done. Now is the time to get to work; but I hope the new commissioner will not let some statements that can be found in this year's report of the superintendent pass unnoticed. On page 47 appears a statement which has been commended by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Jaenicke) as showing a great improvement. He read the statement and believed it; but let us compare the facts with the report. The report states;
One thousand four hundred and eleven convicts out of 1.779, being apparently reformed and leading a normal citizen's life is. I submit, a most interesting achievement. As already stated, the percentage of repeaters-
But here is the catch, in the next eight words:
-as far as penitentiary sentences are concerned, is 20-68.
That would be a really extraordinary record if it applied to all sentences, but it is not so. This would make us believe that, after being discharged, these people were reformed, but it is wrong to compare this figure with the English and United States statistics. When the English reports say that many people have not been sentenced, they do not mean to penitentiaries only but to any gaol or any other penal institution throughout England. Here the acting superintendent gives the picture in the words "as far as penitentiary sentences are concerned." Then latter he says:
Figures show that 79-32 per cent of those discharged went straight.
I do not think that is a fair statement, because of every six men throughout Canada sentenced for crimes, five go to county or local gaols and one goes to the penitentiary. I am sure the superintendent could not bring in the records of these men after investigation
and prove that they had not been sent to other institutions, though they might not have gone back to a penitentiary. Here he says they went straight, because they did not go back to a penitentiary. In England, when they say such men were reformed they mean they were not sentenced to any institution. The same thing applies to the statement made in the report about the El Reno reformatory in the United States. There the records of these men are followed, and if they are said to have reformed it means they have not been sentenced anywhere. In this report, however, we are asked to believe that a man has reformed because he has not been sent back to a penitentiary. I am sure the new commissioner would not make a statement of that kind, to judge by the report he has brought in this year.
To get back to the bill, however, the point remains whether we should have one man or three men to start this work of reorganization which is so badly needed. At first, after a few years in that kind of work in the department, I had the idea that a one-man commission might work along the lines of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Then I realized that in the past we had been very unfortunate in most of the men to whom we had given these considerable powers. On one occasion the three members of the royal commission were in my office, unofficially, and we discussed that point. At that time I understood from them plainly that their survey of the whole penitentiary set-up in Canada had convinced them that three men would be better' than one as far as this type of work was concerned. That was not because they had recommended that provincial gaols and other institutions should be included in the set-up but because they felt strongly that it should be a three-man board. The man the minister told us he would recommend to council for the approval of the governor general appears to be a better man than those we had previously. I have never met him, but his report impresses me favourably. It may be that there will still be the danger suggested by the commission, of giving a man too much power so that he may run these institutions in a dictatorial way, which the penitentiary commission was definitely against in its report; but I am willing to support the bill as it now is in the hope that the man will do what we expect him to do. It has been said that the commission favoured a three-man board because they wanted cu include the other penal institutions; but hon. members may believe me or not, as they wish, when I say that when I spoke to the com-
