missioned they were definitely against the one-man system, even in regard to the penitentiaries themselves.
I could talk on this subject for hours and perhaps bring in a good deal of other material that would be of interest to those who concern themselves in such matters. I believe much has been said up to now in this debate that is good. In my view the new commissioner should be given every opportunity to begin work as quickly as possible.
In conclusion, let me say that the most important thing he has to look into is the matter of staff, the question of obtaining proper staff both in respect of higher officials and even with regard to the lower ranks. The improvement which has been made in the lower ranks can be continued, because some improvement was attempted immediately after the report was brought in.
I would point out that paragraph 12 at page 8 of General Gibson's report states that a group of men was sent to the British training school at Wakefield, and the establishment of a training school in Canada was foreseen in the near future. That was done in 1938 and 1939. It cannot be said it was done between 1940 and 1947. One of the main points is that all preparation and selection of personnel were then made by Doctor Shortt who also recommended the appointment of a special officer, Colonel Megloughlin, to pursue that work.
First of all, I hope those men who will be commissioner, deputy commissioners and assistant commissioners will be chosen very carefully. Few people who had anything to do with the previous administration, at the head office should be included in that. I do not say that the wardens do not deserve to be given a chance to prove good under the new methods of improving the system and their institutions, because I consider they have been handicapped until now.
But at the head office let us clear the ground; let us clear away the dead wood. Let us have men who will understand the problem and who will be able to support the commissioner who has been appointed, or whose appointment is pending.
Then, let us plan for the penitentiary system the buildings which are to be built, and for the repair of others. Old buildings have been readapted, but much has still to be done. It has been done in England, and there is no reason why repairs cannot be made in Canada to some extent on old buildings. But this should be done by people who know better than those who have been handling it up to now.

With respect to new ones, I would advocate that they be built by contract, instead of by penitentiary labour, as has been done in the past. As I stated earlier, a building was started at Laval twenty years ago but has not yet been completed. A penitentiary building which has been planned by experts, whether it is at a cost of $3 million, $6 million or $10 million, will cost less than the institutions we now have throughout Canada. And I would dare any accountant connected with the penitentiary system, or any man from the auditor general's office, to dig out what the penitentiaries branch has paid in the last fifty years in connection with the building cost of the penitentiaries we have had in that time. The cost has been staggering. Yet it does not show, because it has been a case of repairing this and repairing that, and only small amounts each year are included in the estimates. But the total actual cost of each building would frighten the house.
Recommendations which have been made by the Archambault commission show that our building methods are now outdated, according to new theories of penology. Let us see things a little more broadly, and if the new commissioner dares-and he will, if he is given support by the minister, and if the house gives him a chance to bring in his new policy-let him have these institutions built as the modern institutions they should be. They will cost less in the end. They will be better.
Someone will ask what the men will be employed at during that time. There are many things to be done. Prisoners are not confined to the crushing of stone, the laying of bricks, or the putting of one stone on top of another.

With the permission of the house, I should like to conclude. The next item should be the classification of prisoners, something which the commissioner sets out as being most desirable, but which he admits has not yet been done properly. The segregation of prisoners is another point. Then, there is the treatment of the reformables and the incorrigibles. Much is made in the report as to the need of having a reformatory institution in the maritime provinces built after agreement with the three provincial governments, and three other such institutions, one in Quebec, one in Ontario and one in the west, which would be in addition to the regular penitentiaries.
This is far from being a Borstal system. As the minister said, some magic seems to attach to the word "Borstal" in the minds of

Penitentiary Act
many people. But Borstal does not apply to all cases. The fact that we would have a Borstal institution does not mean that all our evils would be corrected. The minister was right when he made that statement. It is only part of a system, and people should not place too much magic in one word. There is a limit to what it can do; it cannot perform miracles, and our system can be vastly improved even if we do not have immediately Borstal institutions.
In connection with the building of these institutions there is one further point, and that is: What will you employ your men at? We could do the same thing as is done in the United States penitentiaries. We could incorporate a crown company which would administer the institutions. We could have workshops and turn out products which could be sold to the government. They could be operated at a profit. At the present time, when the department gets in any money it goes to the receiver general. The institutions could make money from year to year and become self-supporting. In the United States an independent state company has been organized. It is administered independently, but it is under the supervision of the department of justice. This company operates shops in all the institutions. The men are taught trades in the shops, which are operated just as a manufacturer -would operate them. They do not compete with outside manufacturers who are supplying the public. But they do sell to the government at a profit, receiving the same prices which are received by private manufacturers.
The prisoners are employed in this way. They are allowed fair salaries to be given to them when they leave the institutions. I suggest that the idea of a crown company should be surveyed.
Now that we know that General Gibson will be appointed, 1 am prepared to give him full confidence and encouragement. It matters little whether he is accompanied by one man, two men or three men; if he is the right man he can do the job. I am willing to support the bill, and to recommend it. The commissioner should not procrastinate. He should put into operation as soon as possible either the whole report, or whatever portion of it he intends to make effective. I have great hope that he will prove to be the man who can give proper leadership, and for that reason I am -willing to support the bill.

I am glad to see the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard) back in his seat. I always listen to him carefully, and read his speeches, but
an hour- is too much for anyone to speak here on this subject at the present stage of the session. I shall occupy only about ten minutes of the time of the house.
I have sympathy for the minister who has started out in his new department to try to clean things up in connection with prison reform. Nothing was done during the war; although what the war had to do with it, I do not know. I believe those who were in charge of the department were largely to blame.
Prison reform is not connected with a war.
I wish to compliment the minister because he has started out actively to clean up in the matter of law reform. I would thank him for what he has done thus far. I believe that in the minister we have a man who is sincere and one who has rendered splendid service to his country. He is now in a position to do something by way of real prison and law reform.
It is one of the cardinal principles of magna carta that the people should take a large share in the administration of criminal justice. Whether these institutions are managed rightly or wrongly, they are managed solely and entirely by crown officers. Nobody knows what is going on in them; nobody knows night or day what is happening to the poor unfortunates in these stone piles.
This debate has been going on and I noticed there were only eleven members on the government benches, but there are two or three more now. Last night there were twelve on the Conservative benches; there were eight government members up until 10.30 o'clock; there were six C.C.F.; there were two Social Credit members and one or two other independent members; a total of twenty-nine. The number has not increased very much since that time. Is it any wonder that so little is done in connection with this work? Is it any wonder that these things are going on?
The whole question of reform started in Toronto back in 1908 and 1909 when Mr. Hanna was provincial secretary. Three of the newspapers took it up and they kept it consistently before the public. One was the Toronto Telegram; the second was the old Globe under the editorship of the late Harry Anderson, a former member of the press gallery, and the third paper took a great deal of interest in it. What kind of inspection do we have? Members of the House of Commons and of the Senate are on the board of visitors, but how many of us have visited these institutions?
Penitentiary Act

We all know what Mr. Hanna did to clean up the situation in Ontario. The city of Toronto established two gaol farms, one on Yonge street for men and the other at Concord for women, to help close up the Mercer reformatory. The latter is there yet. Many of these institutions were built before confederation. The Don gaol, which is in my riding, was built just a little after confederation. The late Doctor Hastings, the medical health officer, and I visited it, and we both condemned it as being unfit for human habitation, but it is still in use today. Thousands of prisoners go through that gaol every year, many of them who have never been in trouble before. It is not the fault of the fine officials there. The system and plant are to blame. It is a public scandal that prison reform is nowhere. We talk about the magna carta and freedom, but in these institutions there is nothing but fear. They should have the motto over their doors: "Abandon hope all ye who enter here."
Let us look into this problem. The attendance in the house was only twenty-nine up until 10.30 o'clock last night, 216 members being absent. It is up a bit today, but it has never been over thirty-five while this discussion has been going on. The first thing we should do is to appoint twenty-five members to visit these institutions and find out if this report has given value for the expenditure of the money that was made. I have a great deal of sympathy with the gentleman who has been appointed. He has taken hold of this thing. He is a good citizen and a likeable and able man. I shall give him any support I can. and to the two gentlemen the minister has chosen. The report has recommended changes that should have been made twenty-five or thirty years ago but forgets to get on with the Borstal system federally and do something now.
Some sections of the country have been getting relief in connection with these matters while others have not. I remember when the Hepburn government was in power in Ontario in the thirties and early forties. The federal government enacted a measure to assist in the building of municipal institutions by provinces in order to relieve unemployment. In Quebec,
I hree Rivers got a court house; other places in Quebec and other provinces got new schools, new gaols, new roads, new sidewalks, parks and many other things. These were paid for one-third by the federal government, one-third by the province and one-third by the municipality, We did not get a cent of that fund in Ontario because the premier would not permit the municipalities to accept it. The result is that we have a lot of old,
[Mr. Church.1
dilapidated gaols, some of which are not fit for pigpens. The late Doctor Deslauriers, then member of parliament for St. Mary, Montreal, who was here before His Honour the Speaker, said that he found some of these places to be public hazards, and I can say the same myself. After inspecting them, he said they were operated contrary to all known laws of public hygiene.
If these things were known to the general public they would not be permitted to go on for fire minutes. This problem was nearly solved in Ontario and it would have been solved had it not been for the two wars. Penal reform by Howard really started one hundred years ago. After that time Mr. Thomas Fowell Buxton, M.P. in 1818, said:
I am well persuaded that the penal evil exists only because it is unknown; that it arises not from insensibility, on the part of the nation, but from ignorance; and that a faithful disclosure of the scenes which may be witnessed in almost every county jail in England, would speedily be followed by an impulse to prevent them.
Y ou would think that the public of this country, in modern days like these, even after two great wars when everything is topsyturvy, would know what is going on in these institutions. If they did know', d'o you think they would approve? We know how some businessmen try to get off from serving on juries. As I say, Mr. Hanna did a lot toward solving this problem in Ontario. The premier of Quebec has announced the formation of a committee in Montreal to consider conditions there. The provincial secretary's department in Ontario are doing something. Mr. Dunbar opened a school for youthful offenders at Brampton and there is one also at Bowman-ville.
A lot of these people should never be in gaol. Unfortunately we have many magistrates today-I am not referring to those in my city-who like to remand accused persons. They are then sent to gaol until the magistrate takes one or two weeks to make up his mind. Many of these people have never been in gaol before. There should be some change made. I had a bill before parliament which would have remedied this condition, and I hope the minister will do something about it.
I have visited many of the county gaols in Ontario and in many cases the people were too poor to pay their fines. We should adopt the law which was passed in England twenty years ago. Their summary convictions act closed half the gaols in the old country. That act gives a person a chance to find the money with which to pay his fine. All over this country people are in prison because of debt,

Penitentiary Act
a thing which Dickens wrote about when he wrote about Little Dorrit. We have the same condition here in this country. Everybody knows it is wrong, but nothing is done about it. In England when a man is convicted for some petty thing and fined they give him time to pay his fine and he goes home the same night. The bill which I introduced this year had the support of the John Howard society in Canada. They wrote several tetters to me commending the bill, and I hope the minister will give consideration to that bill and the clause regarding time to pay fines, because many people are in gaols who should not be there at all.
Many references have been made in this House of Commons to the Borstal system. I can remember when I first came here; in fact one of the reasons for my coming here was to get something done about this penal institution business. The old gaol in my riding was to be torn down, but I am sorry it has not been. We had the promise of the Ontario government that the moment the two gaol farms were ready they would close it up, but it has not been closed up at all. The excuse is that there would be no place to which to remand prisoners. We could have had a fine new one, if Ontario in 1935 had allowed our city to get funds the way towns and cities in Quebec did, as I mentioned before.
There should be some changes in the law. We have judges complaining about people not wearing hats. Ladies in the House of Commons and in the galleries are not wearing hats. I have seen all kinds of ladies' hats. As I said the other day in the house, some of these hats I see on women are not much larger than the size of the little cartons you get containing a spoonful of marmalade. The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) said that these hats would be too big for certain justices in courts. The other day a boy of thirteen fainted in the witness box in a Toronto court after being obliged to stand in the box for one hour. Why should witnesses have to be in the box at all and not be given a chair? I think the House of Commons should be in the box to find out modern reform.
Regarding some of these other offences, as we are talking about the other fellow, what about the poor fellow who tries to commit suicide? In Rosedale it was a popular occurrence for people who wanted to commit suicide to jump off one of the bridges there when they got that tired spring feeling or were out of work and nobody wanted to be bothered with them. A few days ago a magistrate sent one of these would-be suicides to gaol for
thirty days because a section of the criminal code says that a would-be suicide must be committed to gaol. He needed a hospital, not a gaol. I hope that things like that will be eliminated from the criminal code.
We should long ago have had a legal committee here to consider legal bills, as they have in the provinces. I hope the minister will bring down an amended criminal code. There should be a decennial revision of the code just as there is of the Bank Act, to bring it up to date. We should not leave it the way it is, where nobody knows the law.
Here we are in this House of Commons within two hours of one of these penal institutions and within three hours of another one. Surely twenty or twenty-five members could go through one of these institutions and see what the actual conditions are. The Archam-bault commission on prison reform came about because of Toronto and other members, aided by Toronto newspapers, keeping before this house the need of prison reform. This report, after three years, cost half a million dollars, and only for a few recommendations, still not law.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to this debate and have learned a great deal. I listened with much interest to the speech of the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Jaenicke) and to the brilliant speech made last evening by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). I represent a large number of people and a good number of organizations who are much interested in this problem, and for that reason I wish to make a few comments at this time. I would not for a moment suggest that I could speak with the same authority or knowledge possessed by some other members. But I can say this. I speak personally and for many persons in my district who are much concerned about what is to be done about this problem.
This is not a spectacular bill, not one that creates a good deal of ferment in the country, and apparently not a great deal of interest in the house, but it is an important bill because it is one aimed to do something to assist our unfortunate Canadian citizens in a new way. In doing that, I say that we are taking a step forward in the development of Canadian civilization. In my opinion this bill, together with the remarks made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley), the report of General Gibson, and the speeches of hon. members, indicates that at last something is to be done to implement some of the provisions of the Archambault report.
Over the years I have made it. a point to visit some of these institutions and have
Penitentiary Act

visited in them individuals whom I had known previously in, civilian life. I have talked with them and come away somewhat sad because I realized the unfortunate circumstances that do prevail in some cases. I have felt up until recently that the great majority of the Canadian people were very remote from this problem. I think it has been a question of their not seeing the problem because they were not thinking about it, and those who were concerned were a small number who were interested in it from humanitarian motives, and the relatives of the unfortunate inmates. But I think that situation is changing. I have noticed that appreciably in the last year or two and in this debate in this house, which I think will do a great deal to inform many people in Canada who have not been interested to date in this great problem.
As far as my own experience in my constituency is concerned, I have a personal knowledge of several unfortunate cases, the result I should say of a mixture of impulsive youth, excessive drinking, and in some cases unfortunate companions. I have visited some of these people in the institutions and have talked with their relatives, and more than ever have I become convinced that the time is right to adopt new methods in our penal institutions. I have discussed this question with senior police officials, judges, magistrates and many other people, and the general opinion expressed by those competent and responsible people was that there was a great need for segregation. That is one thing which impressed me in visiting these institutions. There is also a great need for training while in the institution and a great need for after-care. The hon. member for Lake Centre mentioned an unfortunate person who spent some time in a penal institution and reformed and returned to civilian life. For some reason or another there is a stigma attached to those who have paid their penalty to society in a penal institution. I have known several men who could not regain positions because somehow or another some person was mean enough to remind someone that they had served a prison sentence.
I do want to support the plea of urgency that has been made by several members. This is an urgent matter and action should be taken as soon as possible. I am not in accord with some of the severe criticisms that have been made of the proposals in General Gibson's report or the outline given to the house by the Minister of Justice. I prefer to wait for a year or two and see what happens as a result of this legislation.
In concluding, I say that many of us have great hopes, and I hope that, after the passing
	,
of a year or two, we shall be able to commend the minister and his officials upon the results which have been obtained in that time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It will not be necessary for me to say very much in concluding this debate. The bill before the house is a simple one, as I said when I introduced the resolution. The debate lias taken a wide range. I am not sure whet her the rules of the house permit so wide a range, but I did not wish to take any exception to the latitude of the speeches, because I thought the discussion was so useful and I preferred to have it at an earlier stage rather than at a later one in the session.
Much of this discussion would ordinarily have taken place on the penitentiary estimates. Other parts of the discussion would have taken place in the normal course on amendments to the criminal code. However I am grateful to hon. members for expressing their views on so many subjects connected with the administration of the penitentiaries, and for expressing them so frankly and so fully as they have in this debate.
I do not know that it is necessary for me to reply seriatim to the points which have been made by various speakers because, as I have indicated, there will be occasions later in the session when these matters can be discussed more properly than they can be on this bill.
The hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Jaenicke) somewhat sharply challenged the principle of the bill. I think he was the only member who has spoken in the debate who did. He took the position that he was opposed, and that the house should be opposed. to the setting up of a one-man commission instead of a three-man commission. On the resolution I gave the reasons why the government took the view that in the circumstances a one-man commission was preferable. It may be that if all the recommendations of the Archambault report could be carried out the argument for a three-man commission would be stronger; but the main recommendation of the Archambault commission cannot be carried out,
Recommendation No. 1 reads as follows:
The Canadian penal system should be centralized under the control of the government of Canada, with the federal authorities taking charge of all the prisons in Canada, the provinces retaining only a sufficient number to provide for offenders against provincial statutes, prisoners on remand, and those serving short sentences.

Penitentiary Act
I am not convinced that that would be a desirable thing to do. There are a great many opponents of centralization in this country, and a great many who believe that decentralization, even in matters such as this, is preferable. The arguments for decentralization in this field are about as strong as they are in a great many other fields where they are admittedly strong. I am not convinced that that recommendation should be carried out, but even if it should be, I have no reason in the world to think the provincial authorities would be willing to have it carried out.
Will the minister permit a question for the purposes of information? *

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Have the provinces been communicated with recently with a view to ascertaining their position in that regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Not so far as I know. After all, that would involve the taking of a decision by the federal government to press for centralization and the control of all the prisons of Canada. We have been pounded during the greater part of this session whenever we allegedly approached anything like centralization. We have been attacked for desiring to centralize authority by some of the provinces and by a great many hon. members. As I say, I am not convinced that it would be desirable to attempt to vest in ourselves control of all the prisons in Canada. If hon. members wish to advocate that I should like them to take some responsibility for advocating it. I say that if the provinces of Canada desire to discuss that with us we shall be glad to discuss it. They will not find us the least bit stubborn on this point. If they want to discuss the matter we have an open mind on it. But under the constitution theirs is the responsibility, and instead of our reaching out to get more responsibility and vesting it in ourselves, it seems to me it is for the authorities who have the responsibility and who think they should divest themselves of it to approach us, rather than for us to approach them.
As I say, if we could carry out the main recommendation of the Archambault commission's report, maybe the argument would be stronger for a commission of three, but we cannot. I think one-third of the prisoners of the country are under the jurisdiction of the dominion parliament and approximately two-thirds of the prisoners are under the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures, so our field of activity is hardly one that requires an elaborate organization. It is a field of activity where, in my judgment, one commissioner provided, as I said, that he is a good man, is better than three.
In the late thirties we were going in for these three-man boards, five-man boards, seven-man boards and so on. All over the country it was said that they were the salvation. It was said, let us have a board; put the board outside of the control of the government if possible, and certainly well away from the control of parliament, and let it function, as it was said, without any political interference; then we would get efficiency. Now we have had a lot of experience with these boards, and personally I do not believe in going too far. There again the opposition in the house has criticized us for our boards, our commissions, our controllers and so on. If I am to be responsible for the administration of the penitentiary system of Canada I want to be dealing with one responsible official, not with a board. When something goes wrong I do not want to have to find out, if I can, which man or which two men or who it was that was responsible for its going wrong; I want to be able to hold one man responsible instead of an aggregation, which is very much harder to put your finger on. You cannot say that three men are three times as good as one man; you cannot say, the more the merrier, the more the better in these things. You have to pay some attention to the human factor. If you get one good man who is responsible to the minister who, in turn, is responsible to the government and to parliament, in my judgment you get a more efficient organization in a matter such as this than if you set up a board.
The reasons for setting up boards in some instances is to give all the parts of the country representation or something of that kind. There is no such reason here. Therefore I ask the house, which I think it is prepared to do, to support the recommendation of the government in this regard.
It was very interesting to hear the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard) say this afternoon that the former minister had difficulty to get men to accept appointments in this field. It may very well be that if we stuck to the idea of a three-man board we would have a little difficulty getting appointees. That will not be a difficulty with this legislation, because we have the commission set up as soon as the legislation is passed, and at least we shall not have much of an excuse if we do not make some progress in the very near future, as the house and the country expect us to do.

Will the minister permit, one simple question? He mentioned that in the late thirties the practice of estab-

1. Departmental administration, $191)314.

I do not know whether
the minister intends to make any statement on this item. If he does, I shall wait.

I do not know that it is necessary to make any lengthy statement at this time. Matters having to do with agriculture have been under discussion on more than one occasion since the beginning of the session, and I do not wish to cover ground which has already been covered. Probably I should say, however, that there have been some changes in the estimates, as hon. members will see. The general or ordinary vote has been increased by $1,224,135.34, while the special vote has been increased by $1,125,000. The items which go to make up these increases are shown in the estimates, and I do not intend to go into them in detail, but I think I should call attention to two because they do have some bearing upon other items.
It will be noticed that there is an increase of $451,340 in the vote for experimental farms, but I should explain that this represents an amount which was previously in the prairie farm rehabilitation vote and which is now being extended under the experimental farms vote. The amount which has been voted for the St. Mary river dam project, $1,500,000, is a new vote in these estimates. This work was commenced last year and is being carried on this year, with a larger amount being expended.
The only other point I wish to make at this time in regard to the agriculture estimates is that through the administration of the agriculture department we are attempting to carry out the policies which have been laid down during the last few years. In 1944 we brought in legislation which tended to indicate the direction agricultural policy would take throughout the transitional period. I think it was generally agreed that during the last three years of the war agriculture had experienced conditions under which the returns from the activities of farmers throughout Canada were at least as satisfactory as, if not more satisfactory than, they had ever been in the history of Canada. That being so, there was considerable concern as to whether we would be able to maintain that position throughout the transitional period. The government brought forward legislation providing that floor prices might be established under farm products; and during the time the discussions were taking place many hon. members were concerned as to the level of those floor prices in the years immediately following the war. We are able to say definitely that the floor prices which have been maintained are at least as high as the prices of any of our products during the last three years of the war, and much higher than the prices of most products during that period. As a result, the returns from agriculture across Canada on a cash basis have been higher than the average of the last three years of the war, and that condition has prevailed in spite of the fact that the quantity produced has been smaller. In other words, we have had a lower production of dairy products, animal products and feed grain during the years immediately following the war than the average of the period I have mentioned toward the end of the war; yet we have had a higher average return during the last two years than during the preceding two years. The average cash return for farm poduets disposed of by famers during the last three years of the war was about $1,600,000,000.

Supply-Agriculture
The return for each of the last two years was considerably over $1,700,000,000. So I say that as far as returns from farm products are concerned, on a cash basis, in spite of the fact that production was down, the returns themselves have been higher than during the years which we undertook to attempt to maintain our position in relation to them.
The other objective set at that time was to attempt to stabilize prices for farm products, or the returns from farm products, over as long a period of years as possible. That matter has been discussed, in considering other measures, at such great length that I do not think it is necessary to say more than that prices have been stabilized at a higher level in, the months since the end of the war and for some time into the future than was maintained during the last three years of war. That being the case, we feel that the policy as laid down at that time in relation to stabilization has been carried out.
One point I should like to make at this time is that we have also made provision for enlarging upon the plans for rehabilitation. I believe it was two weeks ago I brought down in the house a statement dealing with rehabilitation, not only in relation to the rehabilitation act itself, which applies to the drought area of western Canada, but with regard to rehabilitation in general across Canada. Under the provisions of that statement it is intended to carry on rehabilitation in the drought area with expenditures at least equal in actual amount to the amount expended in the years immediately preceding the war. We intend to set- out the amounts in the experimental farms vote that will be required for certain of the work which previously was carried on under expenditures from the prairie farm rehabilitation vote. To that extent the amount which may be expended on the usual works which have been carried on under prairie farm rehabilitation has been increased.
In addition to that, it was provided that a certain sum would be set up from time to time, either in the general or in the supplementary estimates, to take care of special projects. It was mentioned that among those projects would be some development in connection with marsh lands in the maritime provinces, some development in connection with special projects in British Columbia, and some expenditures in the other provinces across Canada in order to deal with certain developments which were thought necessary for the promotion of agriculture.
I repeat that the first vote of that type which we have in the estimates, which is in
the same form as others to be passed, will be found in item 31, under which vote we have set apart an amount for the St, Mary river dam project. Money will be provided in the same way.
At the time I brought down that statement I was asked a question. I think by the hon. member for Swift. Current. Afterwards, when I saw the question and the answer in print, I realized that, I had not really answered the question which had been asked. We have set up certain methods of dealing with problems which arise in the drought area of western Canada, or what has been known as the drought area. I was asked the question as to whether the last proposal made in the statement issued at that time covered such projects as that which might be put into effect around Elbow on the Saskatchewan river.
Elbow, on the Saskatchewan river, is in the drought area. It might be correct to say that any project which might be undertaken at Elbow would be taken under a vote similar to that with regard to the St. Mary river dam. There is. however, this difference between the two projects, that all the waters controlled by any projects which may be brought into being on the Saskatchewan river are projects having entirely to do with waters having their origin in Canada; whereas the project on the St. Mary river is one which has to do with waters which come directly under the international waters commission. So that the two are not on all fours, but they are both within what is known as the drought area.
The other projects to which I referred in what might be called number 3 in the proposals set out in the statement were projects which were intended to be carried on outside the drought area altogether-along the northern part of the three prairie provinces, anywhere in the province of British Columbia, where it might be considered desirable to proceed with projects, and in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and the maritimes, where it might be considered advisable to proceed with projects. The only projects specifically named were those having to do with marsh lands in the maritimes. and some special projects, which were not determined, in British Columbia. But the third item was intended to cover the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, the northern areas in the three western provinces, and then any other developments of a similar nature which might be brought about in the maritime provinces or British Columbia, all of which would be outside the drought area.
Supply-Agriculture

What progress is being made with the Saskatchewan river project? I have a reason for asking the question, because the possibility of building a bridge across the Saskatchewan river at North Landing depends upon the project. One is anxious to find out what is being done with regard to this project in order that one might know something to tell one's constituents upon returning to his constituency.

I would rather discuss that situation when we reach the proper item, but perhaps I can give information sufficient to serve the purposes of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. The present position of the project is that the engineering necessary to determine whether a dam which can be maintained can be built on the Saskatchewan river has been completed. While I was out west a week ago, I made inquiries as to when we might expect to receive the report in Ottawa. I was told that the report was then with the consulting engineer, who was in Washington, that it was being considered by him and that it was expected back within a short time. In 1939 we were spending some $18,000,000 under the agriculture estimates, and this year we propose to spend $23,202,000. However we must realize that with the increased cost of materials and labour today we shall probably be able only to supply services somewhat below those which were supplied in 1939 with $18,000,000. There have been great shortages of food throughout the world and today Canada is one of the greatest reservoirs of
food in the world. In view of that fact., our expenditures might have been increased to provide an impetus to increase food production in this country.
As the estimates indicate, the increase in expenditures is largely on irrigation projects in western Canada. However, there are many other items in connection with which I think increases would have been justified at- this time. I refer to health of animals, the enlargement of T.B. free areas, more inspection work in connection with Bang's and other such diseases. I think we would have been justified in making much greater expenditures than we are.
The world position today with regard to food indicates the necessity for increased production. Sir John Boyd Orr. speaking at the food conference held at Virginia Springs in 1944, stated that, while science would win the war. food would win the peace. I think we realize today the truth of that statement. We won the war through advances in science, and the conditions in the world today indicate that it will be food that will wrin the peace.
Canada had a remarkably good record for food production during the war. We increased our production of meat products, dairy products, and various other farm products tremendously during those years and at a time when there was a scarcity of help on our farms. But today we find that the increases in. production which we made during the war years are slipping away. In my estimation we should at least be holding the gains we made. I realize, as the minister has stated before in this house, that our increased production of meat and dairy products during 1944 and 1945 were due to quite a large extent- to the fact that when the war started we had surpluses of grains in storage and that during the early years of the war we increased those surpluses until in 1943 we had probably the greatest storage of grain in Canada, we had ever had or probably ever shall have. It. was through the use of those grains that we achieved an increased production of meat and dairy products during 1944 and 1945.
However, as I say, that production has dropped seriously. Last year the drop was some thirty-three to thirty-five per cent in the production of bacon, and there was also a reduction in the production of beef. According to the Department of Agriculture marketing services for May, there was a decrease this year to date of 33-8 per cent in the production of hogs in western Canada, and a decrease of 12-3 per cent in eastern Canada. In beef there was a decrease of 27-2 per cent in western

Canada and a decrease of 1-3 per cent in eastern Canada.- That reduction in produce tion is serious.
It has come to a point, at least in the area which I represent and which is one of the better stock producing areas in western Canada, where our production today is less than it was in 1939. That is a serious situation and one which cannot be justified. To a large degree it has been brought about by the policies of this government. I remember the minister stating in 1940 that the policy of the government w'as to see that we had a diversification of agriculture in western Canada. That stock should be fed on the farm where it was produced, that was the place to finish them. Yet we find that that is not being done today, largely because of policies initiated by this government. These policies are not economically sound. They are not good so far as our western agriculture is concerned, and I doubt whether they help eastern agriculture to any great extent.
This drop in production is, in my estimation, due to two or three definite things which the government has done or failed to do. One of the reasons for the drop in agricultural production in western Canada has been that agriculture is not holding its own in our Canadian economy. I may be asked why I make that statement in view of the fact that, according to the statistical summary of the Bank of Canada, using 1935-39 as the base period, agricultural prices in 1939 were 91-8, while in 1946 they had reached 183-7, or a rate of increase of 100 per cent in the returns to agriculture. But when we give those figures we must take into consideration that the cost of production of agricultural products in 1939 was 99-1, while today it is 149, or an increase of some 50 per cent. We must also take into consideration the fact that in 1939 the average farm income in Canada was only $743. That is a pretty low base from which to start, and even when we have doubled that amount we still have not got very far so far as the returns to agriculture are concerned. The result is that fewer people are prepared to enter agriculture today than at any other period in our history.
In 1941, when we were discussing the Veterans Land Act in the veterans committee of this house, a survey was made to find out the number of boys in our army who would prefer to enter agriculture when the war was over, and out of the first 200,000 who enlisted some 70.000 indicated their desire, when that survey was made, to go into agriculture, even though agriculture had gone through a very much depressed period during the 1930's. But
today, now that our boys have actually returned, a much smaller number of them indicate their desire to enter agriculture. That is an indication that, after their return to Canada, they have looked around and decided that there are other occupations in which the returns are greater than in agriculture, in spite of the fact that the returns to agriculture have doubled during the last six or seven years of the war. Notwithstanding that the returns have doubled and that, according to the bureau of statistics, the net farm income in 1946 was $1,925, we must remember that to earn that net income it is necessary for the farmer to have a capital investment of from $10,000 to $15,000, and when we subtract the interest on that capital investment from the net income we find that the net income is quite small as compared with that of any other group in our Canadian economy. The result is that fewer young people are prepared to enter agriculture today, and the government feel that they must go to Europe to secure people to come to Canada to work on our farms here, because farming is not a sufficiently paying proposition to our own people to induce them to remain on the farm. That is not a healthy condition. It is a condition which, in my opinion, justifies a larger appropriation in our agricultural estimates than is indicated by the increase proposed in these figures tonight.
Another reason why our production of live stock products in western Canada has dropped is the price relationship which grain bears to live stock products. That relationship today is such that it is just not interesting to the farmer to go ahead and produce meat and dairy products, and consequently we find less of them being produced. I am convinced that the new prices announced to the house by the minister on March 17 for coarse grains during the coming season will not get the production that is required. The coarse grains situation in eastern Canada has been indicated today over the radio and in the press. It is forecast that there will be a serious shortage of these grains in eastern Canada. I do not believe that the increased acreage in western Canada, if there is any increased acreage, will supply that deficiency. Take barley, for instance. The price of barley to the farmer today is ninety-three cents a bushel f.o.b. Fort William, and with the present price of hogs and the present price of wheat, I do not think we shall get the increased barley acreage we should have if we are to have the increased meat and dairy production that we need in this country. The government should give serious consideration now to raising the malting premium on barley. We have the lowest malting premium on

barley of any country in the world. The premium in Great Britain and the United States varies from thirty to fifty cents a bushel, whereas in Canada we have a ceiling of 5 cents a bushel on the malting premium that can be paid to our producers. That is not enough to get the increased production we should have. Some may ask, why do you want an increased production of malting barley if it will be made into beer? My answer is that last year when we were trying to get an increased production of meat and dairy products the brewers got all the malting barley they wanted and they will not use any more for such purposes if the premium on malting barley is increased. If it were increased it would induce more farmers in western Canada to produce barley, and more barley would be left over for feed purposes. I am convinced that, until the premium is increased, you will not get the increase in coarse grains that is necessary for an increased production of meat and dairy products in Canada.
Another factor that has been curtailing production in western agriculture is the shortage of machinery in this country and our large exports of farm machinery. Last year I gave the house figures which indicated that our exports of farm machinery had increased tremendously, and that increase in exports has continued this year, with the result that there is a real shortage of equipment in many parts of Canada for the production of agricultural products.
Just before I came here at Easter I visited the local offices of the Veterans' Land Act people. They told me that they had 200 tractors on order which they could not supply. Returned men who had their farms had everything ready to go to work this spring, and yet at Easter they were, in that one area, 200 tractors short of being able to supply what was needed by these men. That is only one small section. There were hundreds of other farmers as well who needed new equipment and were unable to obtain it at that time. In spite of that, we are exporting the largest amount of farm machinery that we have ever exported in Canada's history. I have no objection to exports so long as they are not hindering the production of food in Canada. I do not think machinery shipped to any country in the world will produce more food than it would produce on Canadian farms where we know how to use the equipment and have as good land as there is any other placf in the world. By increasing these exports and 83166-239
selling our own market short, we are not serving either ourselves or the interests of other parts of the world for greater food production.
Another matter which I believe should be dealt with is that of tariffs on farm machinery. The minister may say that we have no tariffs on farm machinery, but that is not a fault. If you look at the old tariff schedule you will find that it was made up at a time when much of the modern equipment which we are using today was not on the market. There are a number of items of new farm equipment which have power attachments which are paying tariff. I need onR' mention some of the newer implements used for the production of sugar beets in this country or the modern hay press which bales the hay as you take it from the windrow, or some of the modern tillage equipment which has a power unit and attachments to operate it, to illustrate my point. This new equipment has come on the market since our tariff schedule was made up, and today it is paying a tariff of up to twenty-five per cent for entry into Canada. Until we are prepared to modernize that tariff schedule, we shall not be giving agriculture in Canada a fair deal; we shall not be giving it the machinery which is necessary for it to compete with production in other parts of the world. They have this equipment in the United States and we should be able to get it here. These are a few of the things that, I believe, should be dealt with if we are to get a greater agricultural production.
Another matter is that of the use of fertilizers in this country. We can increase our agricultural production tremendously by the use of fertilizers. In 1944 I visited England, and I was on a farm where the man was threshing his twenty-fifth consecutive crop of wheat; he was threshing fifty-two bushels to the acre. His statement was that all he required the land for was to hold the plant; that he could feed the land with fertilizer containing everything that was necessary to grow the crop. I did not agree with him entirely, but I do know that they have increased their production in the European countries tremendously by the use of fertilizer. Of course you must have plenty of moisture to do that. In western Canada we can use fertilizer to a limited extent, to the extent only that we have moisture to grow the crops as well as the fertilizer to feed them; but in eastern Canada I am sure that we could, to good advantage, increase the use of fertilizer and thereby raise larger amounts of grain, vegetables and other farm produce. Yet in spite of that, we find the government disposing

of plants that during the war, were used to produce fertilizer. I shall not go into that matter at great length now; we shall have an opportunity to go into it further when we come to that particular item, but that is one of the methods which can be used to increase agricultural production. I am sure that, until we have increased our production, until we have seen that our farmers have equipment, until we have seen that the agricultural economy of this country receives as large a share of the national income as any other group we shall not have successful agriculture in Canada.
The farmers of this country compose 17-3 per cent of the working population, and yet they receive some eleven per cent of the national income. As I said, until some of these things are rectified we shall not have increased agricultural production. I believe that the Minister of Agriculture has the direct responsibility for that. I thank the minister for moving this way. I hope he will continue his movement, and that he will meet us half way or a little more in our requests for a better agricultural policy in Canada. Tomorrow, when reports of this discussion are sent out over the radio and in the newspapers, it may be that once more people will be contending that the farmers all over Canada are becoming millionaires, and I am afraid the figures given tonight will be taken as an indication of a prosperity that does not exist among our agricultural population. A number of people have the idea that living on a farm is all milk and honey, but many of us here in the house tonight realize that farming, particularly this year, is a tough proposition for those actually engaged in it. At the present time I understand not more than ten per cent of the crop around this section of Ontario is in the ground, and I understand that in Quebec the percentage is still lower. So that the farmers of those two provinces particularly, and other provinces throughout the dominion, are facing losses amounting to millions of dollars, because of weather conditions over which they have absolutely no control.
Many people tell us that farmers are much better off than they have ever been before and I am willing to admit that to some extent. But I am still quite conscious of the fact that the farmers are not in as good position as many other occupational groups in Canada. While the improvement in income of farmers ihown by the minister is apparent, it must not
Supply-Agriculture

be forgotten, that at the beginning of the war farming was in a depressed condition, and remained in that state until 1942. To realize that, one has only to look at the amount of debt charged up against farmers at the present time. In addition, we have only to look at. the state of farm buildings, particularly dwelling houses, and the need for improvements in those buildings.
Then again one must consider the situation with respect to the replacement of farm machinery. During the past five years we were not able to buy many machines. By the time the farmers of Canada have reequipped their farms, their financial position will not look nearly as good as it does at the present time. Prices of farm machinery are almost double what they were at the end of the last war; but I do not think anyone would claim that present prices of farm products are double what they were after the last war.
It might be interesting to note that in the period 1915-19 the farmers of Canada, comprising approximately one-third of the population, received thirty-three per cent of the national income. At the present time I understand that we are receiving about nineteen per cent.
Then again, while some people undertake to compare present prices with parity prices, such a comparison is made on a false foundation. The period used is that of 1926-29. At that time the average income received by the farmers of Canada was 16-6 per cent, which is not nearly sufficient for one-third of the population to receive.
I understand that many questions which have been discussed this evening will be discussed again when the different items are called. While it has been the custom for hon. members in different parts of the house to make long statements when departments are opened. I feel that we in this corner are prepared to desist from that practice on the present occasion. Long speeches would only be repeated when the different items are called. For that reason I do not intend this evening to speak at length.
We in this group shall have something to say when the different items are discussed. May I repeat that agriculture is not yet in as healthy a condition as it should be. Until agriculture is a healthy industry, the whole of Canada cannot prosper, and we cannot have that degree of unity to which the people of Canada are entitled. With a prosperous agriculture we could look forward to general prosperity throughout the country.

I should like to speak briefly on the hog question. A discussion has been carried on between the minister and the hon. member for Melfort. While both set out interesting figures, I believe they have thrown a misleading light on the present situation of the Canadian farmer. While those figures may be true, so far as domestic markets are concerned, or revenue from within Canada, everyone will agree that the agriculturist of Canada is the only producer who is tied down in respect of his export market.
Even the farm implement producers export a percentage of their output to other countries of the world at prevailing world prcies. Our lumber producers do that. But the farmer, whose wheat or live stock is exported, is on a control basis, and he does not receive the same percentage of income from his export of goods as does any other producer in the Dominion of Canada. There is still that great difference.
Then, in the matter of hog production, I stated earlier in this session-and no one has refuted it-that the eastern hog producer did enjoy about $9 per hog advantage. That is, the producer in eastern Ontario or Quebec enjoys that advantage over the producer in western Alberta. If it took twenty bushels of barley at twenty-five cents a bushel subsidy to produce a hog, then the eastern producer had an advantage of about $5 in the matter of feed alone. Then there is the difference in freight rates which has not been evened up, and which amounts to about $4 a hog, as between the cities of Edmonton and Montreal. That is another advantage which I do not think anyone will refute.
I wish to ask the minister what control the board, or those in charge of meat, have over hogs marketed and slaughtered in the abattoirs of this country. I believe the board has still some control in order to supply the bacon market of Britain. If it has, I want to know how far that control extends. I ask that because when I was home last Easter, at the St. Boniface stockyards across from Winnipeg there were a great many sows heavy with pig at those abattoirs at that time. I also read reports in the Regina press to the effect that the same thing was taking place in Regina; and I read reports from other marketing centres where people were marketing their brood sows heavy with pig at that time. So I presumed that if the government had the control over this situation it was supposed to have-and I understood it still had that control-it would be able to tell me approximately how many of those brood

sows were marketed at each centre. But the answer I got was that the Minister of Agriculture had no information.
I say the meat board should be able to obtain some approximate information on the question I asked. I trust the minister will tell me to what extent these controls exist today, and why it was not possible for the department to get at least approximately the information for which I asked. I know that in April of this year a great many brood sows were marketed in western Canada, probably for various reasons to which the minister has referred. All this does not come within his own department.
My colleague, the minister for Portage la Prairie-
The minister?

I should say the member; but I am satisfied he will be a minister, at the first opportunity. However, he is still the member for Portage la Prairie. In his maiden speech he asked that farm producers in Canada should be exempt to the extent of S500 for the production of hogs and dairy products. In my view that was a worth-while suggestion, and, while it does not come within the purview of the Minister of Agriculture, it is under the control of one of his colleagues. I know there are some difficulties in the present situation.
There is another matter which will be discussed more fully under the marketing item, which arises from the fact that we have been prevented from marketing our beef cattle in the United States, the greatest natural market Canada has ever had. True enough, we do ship to the market in Great Britain, at a controlled price; but if we were able to market our cattle in the natural market offered in the United States we would be obtaining over fifty per cent more for those cattle than we are allowed by exporting them to Great Britain.
The point I should like the minister to deal with is that of the control on the marketing of hogs, in order to supply the British market; and I wish to know why I cannot have information with respect to the marketing of brood sows in western markets.

With respect to the first question, the extent of the control at present is that the meat board are taking from the inspected plants about eighty-five per cent of the amount delivered in 1940, and that amounts to about forty-five per cent of the marketings at present. They are taking about forty-five per cent of the marketings in the inspected plants; they are not enforcing any
regulations with respect to uninspected plants. That product from the inspected plants is being sent to Great Britain.
With regard to the record of the sows marketed while in pig, I doubt very much if it would be possible to provide any record which would be useful. There is an estimate made from time to time, which shows that the number being marketed is not greater and has not been greater during the early part of this year than in normal times, if these times could be called anything but normal. If anything, they are a little less. Of course, that does not bear out the suggestion that sows which had been bred were being marketed in great numbers in the early part of this season. Again I would say that I do not think any check can be made which would be sufficiently close to be able to say that across Canada there has or has nGt been five or ten per cent more or less marketing of sows. I say that in view of the fact that records cannot be kept, or they have not been able to keep records which were reasonably near the facts; such records have not been kept and hence have not been made public.
These are important questions in relation to production. While I had not intended to get up to say it, while I am on my feet I will say that I agree with the hon. member for Battle River and the hon. member for Souris that certain statements put out, if not followed up by other information, give a wrong impression with regard to the prosperity of farmers. For example, thirty mortgage companies put out a statement a short time ago that the mortgage owing to those companies on farms in western Canada had been reduced twenty-one per cent last year as compared with the year before, and that the mortgage indebtedness was down to a level lower than it had been for a long period of time. Those statements are both true.
But what is of as great importance is the fact that statements with regard to farm income do not bear out the suggestion that farmers in the Dominion of Canada are well off as compared with other people. I have before me a record of farmers' income tax payments which was partly placed on the record in reply to questions asked. I think this should be put on a little more fully and if the committee will permit me I will place this on Hansard.

While the number of returns brought in have been greatly increased it has been found that not more than seven per cent of all the farmers in Canada were making an income which the inspectors thought sufficiently large to pay income tax or to be checked further with regard to whether or not they should pay. With those facts before us, I do not think there is anyone in the committee who will say that our farmers are rolling in wealth. They are not rolling in wealth.
There is no question about it that ninety-three per cent of the farmers did not have a net income of 11,200 in those years. Now that the net income has been increased to $1,500 for a married man on a farm, the number will probably be less rather than more. We are not in position to say that our farmers are rolling in wealth. This brings me to the suggestion made a few moments ago by the hon. member for Souris that an additional $500 exemption should be given to those producing hogs, and, I presume, to those producing dairy products as well. If ninety-three per cent are not now making enough to pay income tax, I do not think that would do any good. I think you will find that the ninety-three per cent are the ones who are producing nearly all the hogs and dairy products.
There are a few large producers near the cities who are making good profits selling milk or perhaps raising hogs when they are able to get refuse as feed from the city. Some of

them are making enough to get into the income tax brackets, and all of those will be found in the 3-7 per cent of farmers I have mentioned. The others who are questionable and who would raise the percentage to seven per cent, if the statements turned in by the inspectors are correct, would probably include many more of the same group. The producers of great quantities of wheat provide part of the number.
Only ten per cent of the beef produced in this country is produced on what would be considered large ranges. Ninety per cent is produced by the farmer who raises two or three or a dozen steers-you might go as high as twenty steers-but he is not the man who is paying income tax. The large ranchers produce only ten per cent of the beef produced in this country, the remainder is produced on the small farms. As one goes out through Ontario it is an exceptional thing to find a farm with more than two or three sows. They do not grow enough feed to feed more than the pigs from two or three sows and at the same time feed a milking herd of, say a dozen cows. Even to feed that number of animals they have to buy half their feed grains from western Canada. Half the grain fed in this province is shipped here from western Canada in order to produce that stock. But it is on those farms with those small herds and that small number of sows that nearly all the cattle and pigs marketed

Might I say that what hon. members have said about the income tax is quite right. About $500 is quite feasible. I have advocated something like that myself. In fact I advocated that there be no income tax on the hogs raised or the cream produced. It is not the income tax the farmer has paid or what he is likely to pay yet. When you send a bunch of inspectors around you scare the daylights out of the farmer. He is producing hogs and butter as an overtime job, just as the industrial worker in the city gets paid overtime for after-hours work. Hog production on a small farm, where most of the hogs come from and where most of the cream for butter is produced, is done by the farmer working fourteen hours a day. If you assure that man who is producing these necessities of life that he will not be taxed on his overtime production, the production will go up by leaps and bounds. Would the minister answer my question?

To answer the last question first, I do not think the government should attempt to tell the farmer just what he can do on his farm. If we attempted to do that we would get into a great deal of trouble. I think most farmers know-I am sure they do, because I talk with them when I go out-they are nowhere near the income tax brackets on a basis of $1,500 of net income. All one needs to do is to take the figures I have given of the number of farms and divide that into the gross income, leaving aside the fact that there is more than one man working on a farm, to find that the whole cash income plus the amount of produce which is used on the farms only produces an average of about $2,300, and all the costs of operation have to be taken out of that $2,300 to obtain the net average on farms all over Canada.
