These inspectors have the minister's ability to make black look white.

Let me go back to the figures. One-half of one per cent paid income tax in one year, one per cent in another year, and 2-14 per cent in another year. The highest number ever was 3-7 per cent. If the farmer has not the income to pay income tax on, there are not many of them going to pay it, and I do not see how any inspector can collect it. He may make the farmer very angry, but that does not mean he collects the money, and the record's show that he is not collecting the money.
With regard to hogs, a certain percentage remains for domestic use and all the others go to the British market, as has always been the case since we entered into agreements to market hogs in Britain. In so far as east and west are concerned, practically all the A's in Canada and the greater part of the B-l's go to the British market, but the percentage of B-l's which go from the west is higher than the percentage of B-l's which go from the east. The reason is that the domestic market in eastern Canada is very much greater than it is in western Canada.
You would not say they are better hogs in the west?
I would not go so far as to say that, although I might think it.

I am always pleased when we reach the agriculture estimates and have the minister on the other side of the house, because he conducts his department with great ability, and I say that without meaning any reflection on the other ministers. When I heard the minister reply in such vigorous terms to the hon. member for Melfort I felt that he was trying to decry that hon. member's statements. The hon. member for Melfort had indicated that the farmers were not well off, and the minister came back and put figures on the record as to income tax. I want to go farther and substantiate that the farmers today are not well off. I have here a report of the research department of the United Farmers of Canada, which gives figures for the province of Saskatchewan taken from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. In 1944 farm capital was $1,152,826.000.	The average per farm was
$9,036. The value of farm buildings in 1941 was $152,286,600. In other words, the value has increased until in 1944 it stood at $172,705,946. This gives ns an average per set of buildings of $1,235. The value of farm implements and machinery, including trucks and cars, was estimated in 1940 at $142,754,000, or

an average per farm of $980.50. I just made a flight out west and I saw a lot of buildings on that flight. The condition of our farm buildings is deplorable. I also drove across two of our prairie provinces. Western agriculture may be in the best position that it has ever been, but we have a long way to go to rehabilitate our farm people before we can be in a position to say that we have done an adequate job.
The chief thing I wish to say tonight is that I feel sure that many parts of the western provinces will have a small crop this year. In the southwestern parts of the provinces continued blowing and drought conditions exist. When I first came to the House of Commons I advocated the principle of an ever-normal grant. At that time the minister of agriculture rose in his place and said that the Liberal party had talked about this principle before there ever was a C.C.F. May I say that so far no plans have been made for adequate storage of feed grain to take us over the lean years. Because of the conditions which exist in eastern Canada today where there are flood conditions and where, according to press reports, we shall get only a thirty or forty per cent normal crop, and since we are already scraping the bottoms of our bins, it is high time that we had a little bit of statesmanship in our government to realize that in good years everything should be done to store in vital places seed and feed to carry our live stock and to provide seed for next year. Nothing along this line has been done. It is not sufficient to talk about it. We have to plan; we have to put a real plan into effect where these things would be integrated.
Another reason for my rising tonight was to say that something should be done _ to increase production in this country. During the war the government asked our farm people to produce supplies of food and grains, not only for our own armies, but for our allies. The results were marvellous, not because of particular planning by the government, but because the Canadian people put their hands to the wheel. The older people and all our people really went to work; but the fact remains that little has been done to make sure that we shall maintain a sort of scientific production or stability in agriculture.
In the other departments of our natural resources we have developed our assets; we have cut our forests; we have gone into the bowels of the earth and taken out our resources of minerals and depleted them. We have done the same with our soil. All these things were put here, as some of us believe, by God as a trust. In the last forty or fifty years we have depleted the fertility of our s >il. It is not

that we have not scientific data from the departments of agriculture in this country. If we properly conserve our soil we can maintain its fertility, but we have not instituted a policy to maintain that fertility.
On February 10, 1947, I spoke on the fertilizer situation in this country. There is a background to that whole problem. One of the chief reasons why we are not using fertilizer today is that the price has been too high for farmers in western Canada. It is true that they have got along one way c. another without it, but in eastern Canada, where it is used generally for the production of feeds and other things, the reason it has been used is that it is a necessity. The soils are such that certain ingredients have to be added to them to build up the fertility to grow these products. What is happening in the west? We are depleting the soil. Unless we can get a policy wrhich will conserve the soil for posterity, we shall have deserts in many of these places. I state candidly that < his government have betrayed the organized farmers, in fact all the people of Canada bjr the way in which they have handled our war plants and by selling them out to private industry. It seems to me that the government have been seduced by capitalism and have gone down the path and sold out to them rather than keep the interests of the Canadian people at heart. It is not only the farmers' problem; it is the problem of everybody who eats in Canada, because unless we can produce food and supply our people with cheap food not only will it be too bad for our own people in the low income brackets, who are today undernourished, but also statesmen realize that, unless we can produce food and supply the other nations, we shall not have peace. That is the only way we can help to establish peace, because so long as you have starvation and hunger you will not have any sort of stable peace in the world. Therefore I say we should have established the principle of maintaining one of these fertilizer industries to produce cheap fertilizer for the farmer.
I wish to put on record the situation with regard to fertilizer in Canada. There are three ingredients which enter into the manufacture of fertilizer. Before the war, the compound which is most costly, nitrogen, was obtained from our coke plants and other steel industries. When the war came, the government built three large plants, one at Trail, one at Calgary and one at Welland. The government gave an undertaking to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture that, after the war, one of these plants would be kept to produce fertilizer for the farmers. One of the facts 83)06- -240 J
which have come out is that, before the war, sulphate of ammonia, which is a by-product of the coke mills, was sold for $21 a ton. This was chiefly handled by Canadian Industries Limited. All that the company did was to take this material from central Canada and hand it over to the mixing plant at $33 a ton. Therefore, even though the cost of transportation would be about $2 a ton, they made around $10 a ton. The mixture was sold at around $44 a ton, with the nitrogen going into fertilizer.
During the war through experiments it was found that the Welland plant, the Calgary plant and the Trail plant could produce a new type of nitrogen for fertilizer. When I pointed this out in the earlier debate on February 10 the minister said that we would have to export a lot of this nitrogen if we kept one of these plants. I wish to ask him now what is wrong with exporting some of it if we could produce cheap fertilizer for our own people in Canada? The government sold the plant to the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company at a greatly reduced price. The original plant of the North American Cyanamid cost approximately $19 million, and it was sold for $4,750,000. Is it realized the profits that this private company is making? I hold in my hand a list of the profits that the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company showed in 1946. They amount to $23,323,168, or $7.12 a share. This was an increase in profits of 100 per cent over 1945. Then it goes on to say that the chief reason for the increased sales was the greatly increased use of fertilizers. In the investigations which have been made by university men, to whom we pay good money to find out what these fertilizers can mean to us, it has been found that, by using them, we can produce eight to ten bushels more per acre. That being so, I wonder why it is not good business for this government to see to it either that our farmers are subsidized so that they can use fertilizers, or that we at least keep a plant and provide fertilizers to our farmers at cost. This has been dealt with by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Even one of the hon. members to my right, as far back as 1941, asked the Minister of Agriculture at, that time why the price of fertilizers had been "upped" $12 a ton. I understood the minister to say he was going to look into that and see what the reason was but, as I understand it, he has never given an answer to the house.
We subsidized the use of fertilizers after that, during the war period.

Yes, but why did the price go up at that time? That is the point. As I indicated in this house

before, prior to the war we had a world cartel in the production of fertilizer, and today here we have the government selling the Canadian farmer and the Canadian people out to these cartels, so that once again we have the growth of monopoly in this country. I feel this has been a sell-out. Here we have the North American Cyanamid people and Canadian Industries Limited who control the production of fertilizer in this countiy. I think I should put on record part of the agreement which this government made with the Welland plant and Alberta Nitrogen Products Limited. I am going to read it into the record, if I may. Hon. members will recall that when the minister was approached by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and asked that one of these plants be maintained, he stated that his [DOT]understanding was that one of them would be kept; and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply said the same thing. Going back as far as the recommendations of the war expenditures committee, a request was made that the contracts with these companies be renegotiated, so that these plants might have been kept by the government. Nothing was done about that. As I said before, I am just going to read this into the record. This is the disposal of plant clause in the government contracts regarding the fertilizer plants at Welland and Calgary, and reads as follows:
If hereafter for any reason the (U.IC.) government at any time or times within twenty (20) years from the date hereof shall desire or determine to lease or dispose of said plant or any department or part thereof except to "any government within the British empire or North America," N.A.C.L. shall be given the first opportunity (for a period of ninety days after receipt of written notice stating the determination of the government to lease or dispose (as the case may be) of the same and the material terms upon ivhich such lease or disposal will be made) to lease or purchase (as the case may be) the same upon as favourable terms as the government is then willing to accept therefor before the government shall lease or sell the same to any other party except as aforesaid and the government will not at any time during the twenty (20) year period lease or sell said plan or any department or part thereof to anyone (except as aforesaid) on terms less favourable to the government than offered to N.A.C.L.
This is article XII of an agreement between the United Kingdom government, the Canadian government and the Chemical Construction Corporation and the North American Cyanamid Limited dated August 26, 1940.
I might say that a similar agreement was made with Alberta Nitrogen Products Limited. Another clause of the agreement was that this plant would have free use of patent rights on everything which had been discovered during the war. As I said at the beginning of my speech, I think this government has failed

organized agriculture and has failed the citizens of Canada by not keeping one of these plants, at this time when we are scraping the bottom of our bins and when we may be facing a tragic situation this fall in the way of having no feed for our live stock, loss of seed and lack of production to feed a hungry world. If we had done this, I think it would have been one really constructive step toward maintaining production in this country.

Yes. That is the proper place for any general discussion on any particular item. A general discussion on fertilizers is proper when the fertilizer item comes up, and a general discussion on the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is proper when we come to that item. I should like to ask the minister one question with regard to hog production in western Canada, upon which I am far from clear after listening to his arguments. As a matter of fact, it seems to me that he has argued himself around in a circle and down into a gopher hole which, has no back door.
All gopher holes have a back door.

There is occasionally one where the gopher has not had time to build a back door, and I think that is the kind the minister has got into. The minister has stated, and produced a great many figures to show it, that the level of income tax has nothing material to do with the reduction in hog production in western Canada. He also produced a great many arguments to show that it pays the farmer about twenty-five per cent better, I think his figures were, to feed his barley and other coarse grains to hogs rather than to market them. In spite of all those arguments, the fact still remains that the farmers of western Canada have been going backwards steadily as far as the production of hogs is concerned. The thing has apparently been falling off for the past three years. If the arguments the minister has advanced are correct I should like him to explain why this reduction has been going on so steadily. In other words, what is the reason that we are not producing more hogs, or anything like the number of hogs we should be producing in .western Canada?

I should like to say a word on this same question. As the minister knows, before the war the people of eastern Canada were continually urging the farmers of the west to go into live stock more heavily, but at that time government policy and the price situation did not encourage this. Then, during the war there was a tremendous increase in the production of hogs in western Canada, partly as a result of government policy and partly as a result of price increases. A few years ago, however, the farmers of western Canada got the idea that the government actually wanted a reduction in the production
of hogs. I do not say they should have got that idea; the minister quickly made it clear that this was not government policy, but the farmers had that idea. The point I should like the minister to clarify is .this. Is it the policy of the government today that the production of hogs in western Canada should be maintained at the present level rather than increased, thereby making a greater percentage of the coarse grains available to eastern Canada? I ask that question because, in spite of what the last speaker said, I believe that we shall see an increase in the production of hogs in the west. I know that in my own part of the country all the farmers seem to be increasing the number of their brood sows once more, and I am wondering whether or not that will be a wise policy. Does the government think it is wise to bring about an increase in the production of hogs in western Canada during the next four or five years? Will the result be a glut; or would it be better to maintain the production of hogs there at present levels and allow more coarse grains to come to eastern Canada?

The policy of the government and of the Department of Agriculture is, the more hogs produced in Canada, the better for the farmers. Too many people are circulating the idea that we are producing these hogs for the purpose of feeding somebody. The purpose of the farmer is to make as much income as he can on his farm, while producing food. The suggestion was made by the hon. member for Calgary East that I had used figures and arguments to show that the farmer could make twenty-five per cent more by feeding his hogs in Alberta than by selling the grain. I did not produce any such arguments. I said there were advertisements over the radio in Alberta, by a farm organization, in which this statement was made. There were advertisements in Alberta newspapers, of which I have copies. In those advertisements the farm cooperative is saying to the farmer, "You can make twenty-five per cent more feeding your grain to hogs than by selling it. Feed hogs." Those are not my figures; they are the figures of the farm organization in Alberta.
On the other question, as to why hog production has been down, that has always been so obvious to every farmer in Canada that I cannot understand why even people who do not feed hogs should not understand it as well. The reason is that it takes grain to feed hogs; and I do not know of any better reason than the fact that there is not enough grain to feed any more hogs.

There was always enough in western Canada.
Supply-Agriculture

There is not enough there if western Canada sells it. On the question of whether or not we want the western farmer to produce grain for the eastern fanner, the answer is definitely no. We want the western farmer to feed hogs on his own farm; at least we are suggesting that it would be a good thing for him to do so. We are not pleading with him to do it; we are simply saying to the western farmer that his own cooperative is saying, "It will give you twenty-five per cent more return, even as far away as Alberta, and it will give you a higher return the closer you get to the market, if you feed grain to hogs instead of selling the grain." That is what the farm organizations themselves say, and we repeat it, using their figure. After we have said that, however, if the farmer still continues to sell a considerable part of his feed grain, we shall not criticize him for doing so. After all, a great deal more is involved than merely the question of having the grain. A man must have labour, and he must be prepared to divide up his day in a different way from the way in which he would divide it up if he were selling grain. I said last week in Saskatoon, and I am going to repeat now, that I went west, as did many other farmers out there, because I had become tired of getting up at half-past four or five o'clock in the morning, milking from half a dozen to a dozen cows, feeding the pigs, getting a team of horses ready and out in the field by seven o'clock; then working until five o'clock in the evening, having my lunch and going back to the field again to work until sundown; then coming in and feeding the pigs again. That is why a lot of us went west. We felt that we could grow grain out there and would not need to milk the cows or feed the pigs.
Some of us kept to that opinion pretty well until 1942. Then we had a crop of coarse grains twice as large as any we ever grew before, with just as much wheat as we grew in the best years we ever had; and nobody wanted it. No one except Britain wanted the wheat, and Britain wanted 200,000,000 bushels of it, We produced 560.000.000 bushels in one year, and at the end of the season we had in the elevators 600.000.000 bushels for which we had no market, with another crop about to be marketed in August of 1943. Under those circumstances we said to the farmers, "If you want cash now, feed your grain to hogs and cattle. But if you can get along without cash now, keep the grain stored. Call it an ever-present granary, or whatever you like, but keep the grain Stored either on the farm or in the elevators. At the end of the war you will be able to sell every bushel of it

at a higher price than you have sold your grain for a long time." The farmer did just that. He fed an enormous quantity of pork and beef in 1943 and 1944 on grain he could not sell on the market. He could not get any price for grain at the time, except what the government gave him by way of allowance when he put it in the elevators. The government did not sell the wheat until years later.
Then someone says, "Well, why didn't we keep the ever-present granary?" There is not a member in this house who did not get up in 1945 and 1946, or who did not agree with those who did get up, insisting that this government ship every bushel of wheat, every bushel of oats and every bushel of barley we had in the country to Europe in order to feed starving people. There is no house of commons that would have permitted the government of any country, under the circumstances existing in 1945 and 1946, to keep grain in its bins and elevators. So of course the grain was shipped out to feed starving people, and you could not feed as many hogs in this country with our elevators empty and our bins on the farms empty, with only a month's supply of feed in the middle of the summer of 1945, about the same in 1946, and a little more at the present time. You could not produce any more hogs and cattle than have been, produced; you could not produce any more dairy products than have been produced. I repeat that I do not understand why people keep on arguing the point. They are just as bad as the editor of the Free Press was in connection with the pigs. You cannot breed pigs in March and have them on the market in April of the same year; and you cannot finish pigs unless you have grain. We have not had the grain. Only this morning Mr. Kennedy made the announcement that, unless something unforeseen happens, unless something happens that has never happened before, Ontario will have [DOT] only one-third of a crop of feed grain. Out west, fortunately, we have been able to get in our crop in fairly good condition, two weeks later than usual it is true, but it is not yet impossible for us to have a good crop. And to anyone who asks me in this house, "Are you going to plead with farmers out west to feed all the grain they grow this year", I say that so far as I am concerned, if the condition develops which Mr. Kennedy says is going to develop in Ontario, we shall not insist on any such thing. We shall ask the farmers of western Canada to help the farmers of eastern Canada to finish their live stock. And I have no doubt that when the western farmer requires support and assistance again, as he did in the thirties-if indeed he ever

Supply-Agriculture
requires it agaiu-because of a continuation of crop failures, the people of eastern Canada will be just as helpful to him as we shall ask the people of western Canada to be to Ontario this year, if there is a shortage of feed in Ontario.

The first part of the minister's argument was one which personally, coming from the west. I resent very much. It actually came down to this: His statement really was that the farmer in the west is too lazy to feed hogs, and that that is why production has gone down. As a man from the west, 1 am surprised that the minister, who also comes from there, would make that argument. I am very much surprised, because in my opinion that is not the reason for it at all.
What the minister is trying to cover up is his own wrong oat and barley policy, a policy which convinced the farmer in the west that it paid him better to sell grain than it did to feed it to hogs. The. farmers saw their neighbours feeding hogs with grain which they bought at ten or fifteen cents less than the western farmer could sell it for. or feed it for; and the result was that western farmers refused to feed their grain to hogs. They preferred to sell it.
In my opinion one of the reasons the farmers of western Canada are still not producing anything like the number of hogs they did produce is that they are still convinced, despite the advertising the minister has mentioned. that it, pays them better to sell their grain than to feed it.
In other words, this government policy, so far as grain is concerned, is responsible to a large extent, and not the laziness of the farmer.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.
Does he believe a man is lazy who does not wish to get up at halfpast four o'clock in the morning and work until as late as ten-thirty o'clock at night?
But they all do it.
But he does not need to be considered lazy if he does not W'ant to do it.

That does not enter into the matter at all. If the farmer of western Canada, as I know him, can secure twenty-five per cent more through feeding his grain to hogs, then he will certainly feed it, as soon as he is convinced that that is so. The whole thing is that he is not convinced of it. Whether it is so or not, I do not know. The minister
has been most evasive about it. I suggested he had stated that farmers could make that much more. Then, however, he got up immediately and said that he did not say that.
Another argument he put up was that we did not have the grain. So far as the western Canadian farmers are concerned, they certainly had the grain. We might not have had it in Canada as a whole, but so far as the Alberta farmers are concerned, they had it. They could have fed it, and finished the hogs right there. The reason they did not do so was the government's coarse grain policy. The minister should be prepared to admit that it was his policy to a large extent which has driven the farmer-and particularly the farmer in Alberta-out of hog producing. He should not try to put the blame on the farmer for not being willing to get up early enough in the morning.

Mr. Chairman, usually I am a mild mannered man, and only rarely is that fact abused by some people. I had not intended to say anything in the general discussion of the minister's estimates. But when a few minutes ago he went out of his way to see if he could pick a scrap, I felt I should say something. And I want to tell him this much, that if he wants one we are here to give it to him.
No sooner had he resumed his seat after accusing some of us in this group of taking part in a deliberate plan which was not according to the best principles of the house, than those who agreed with him carried on the discussion.
Let me say this much, that the short speech of the hon. member for Assiniboia was just as much in order on this item as was anything we have heard since, and a good deal of what we heard before. I could point to a number of places in the discussion which has just concluded where the minister could have taken the same exception. After the hon. member for Assiniboia had spoken as briefly as possible in giving a general resume of the situation in respect of agriculture, he concluded his remarks by referring to one subject to which he had given special study. The minister thought that was the time to pick the quarrel.
We are just as pleased as anyone could be that we have an opportunity to discuss the estimates on agriculture with a man who has given considerable thought and attention to the department of which he is the head. As I have said in previous sessions, when I have complimented him, even though we do not always agree with him we are prepared to credit him with knowing his department. But
Supply-Agriculture

we do object to his trying to tell us when and where we should question the administration of his department.
The minister referred to the reason a number of people had gone to the west. Let me say that I was born in the middle western states and I did not need to go west; I went north, along with my parents. The part of western Canada in which we settled, and in the area for many miles around, extending up into the district represented by the hon. member for Melfort, up into the Prince Albert district, into the northwestern part of the province, and right down into that part of the province represented by the minister himself, has never been a straight grain-growing proposition.
There are too many people with the false impression that farmers in western Canada are only grain growers. Ever since I have been in the area I have described, we have had mixed farming. During the years in which we opened up and developed that country, we produced enormous amounts of foodstuffs. We did not mind the hard work; we were prepared to put in long hours. But we did object when the rest of the nation was not prepared to give us a decent wage for the work we did.
I contend that that is where the great difficulty has been all these years. As I have said before in the house, even in the times of so-called wartime prosperity the farmers of this nation have not received a fair share of the national income. Even during the time when they were not receiving a fair share of the national income, no matter what branch of agriculture they are lending their efforts to, you find that in between there is no attempt made to have a proper relationship of the commodities that are produced.
I have contended all the time that we should have a system of parity prices which would give the farmers a fair share of the national income and provide a fair relationship between the prices of the things they have to buy and the things they have to sell. There must be a fair relationship between the various products the farmers produce. I contend that when the minister and his department lend their efforts to providing a fair and square deal for the farmers, when they make that parity price possible, then it will be found that the farmers will go to work and produce the things best suited for the farms that they have.
I contend that it would be foolish to urge the man who has a wheat farm and who possibly cannot afford to spend $1,000 to drill a well to obtain water to go into hog or cattle raising. In many parts of the west there is land more adaptable to the raising of coarse grains than to the raising of stock. The farmers have common sense enough to know

what is the best thing to do with their own land if they are only given a decent chance. The trouble is that there is continuous jockeying, an effort to get the farmer to produce as much as he can for as little as you can get him to take for it.
The farmers have made up their minds that they are going to have a different deal from what they have had in the past. The estimates of the Department of Agriculture are the most important that we have to consider in this session. Whether it is considered on this first item or on the last item, in so far as I and my colleagues are concerned we are prepared to cooperate with the minister if he wants cooperation. But I contend that "cooperation" to be effective must be used both ways.

department carry on any broadcasts or is that done by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation?

Are you putting out any new pamphlets this year? I believe most of the ones you put out date back pretty far.

That would include your monthly reports?
Yes.

When I spoke during the budget debate on May 12 I suggested that either the Department of Finance or the Department of National Revenue put out a booklet to inform the farmers of the proper procedure to be followed in making out fairly accurate income tax returns. Would the minister consider putting out a booklet of that kind? When discussing the same question previously the minister referred to a number of expense items that could be included and he also enumerated other items that could go on the other side of the farmers' account.

I understand that the Economic Annalist does give a considerable part of that information. I would suggest that probably this is not the department that should be putting out information with regard to income tax or the manner in which the forms should be filled out. That is really the task of the national revenue department, and I am afraid that we would be exceeding our functions if we were to go into that field. The other night, when I was out west, I did put out what I would suggest is the proper procedure to be followed. If our farmers generally would do what some farmers do, keep a very simple record themselves, they could save themselves a lot of money. I am told that farmers are being charged from $5 to $25 to have these forms made out to prove that they do not need to pay income tax. There is a
much simpler method of doing it than that. I know the difficulties. The trouble is that the farmer puts in long days. But if he could sit down each evening or once a week and put down what he has paid out and what he has taken in, and then glance at the list of items that are properly chargeable to expenses as indicated in the statement I made tonight, which is put out by the department from time to time, I would say that in ninety-nine out of a hundred cases the farmer himself would find out whether at the end of the year he would be liable for income tax. Most of them are $200 or $300 away from having the necessary income. They can determine with a system of accounting that is very simple whether they are in the income tax brackets, and I think that is the only way in which a farmer can save himself expense in connection with income tax returns. I did say this, that I was certain that if a farmer did that and sent in his statement of what his position was to the income tax authorities in his own district he would save the department the expense of sending out inspectors.
I did not quite finish the statement I was making a while ago and I should like to finish it now. I think the department has done the farmer a good turn in sending out twenty-five inspectors from the different offices in western Canada. I run into persons all over Canada, some of them members of this house, whom you just cannot convince that a farmer is not making enough to pay income tax. People hear stories about the farmer selling so many thousands of bushels of grain, so many cattle and so many hogs, and they conclude that the farmer must be in the income tax brackets. I do not know how they figure it out. The inspectors have gone out and proved to their own satisfaction that the farmer it not. That is a good thing for the farmer, and I think that the more often we repeat the facts that have been found by the inspector, the better. Eventually we may come to the conclusion that it. does not pay to send out so many inspectors. An experienced inspector just requires to take a look at many of the farms to see that they could not make enough to pay income tax.

I have already made my suggestion to the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Agriculture, and perhaps the three departments will cooperate to put out this booklet. I am satisfied that the farmers are quite willing to pay their fair share of income tax, but I am not satisfied that the farmers should pay a tax on the basis on which it was levied during the years 1941 to 1945, and I am speaking from my own personal
Supply-Agriculture

knowledge. If they were given the information in a small booklet it would not cost very much and you would have far better co-operation from the farmers and a lot less hard feeling, but of course that must go hand in hand with proper prices for the things the farmer has to sell.
We put out a booklet which the farmer can get for ten cents, and if he just fills in the columns and puts down the items weekly he can make a complete report.
What is the name of that booklet?
The Farmer's Account Book.
At page 81 of the details in the main estimates I find provision for a supervisor of race track betting. What does that fellow do? I have been intrigued by that detail for some time.
